item.title: Evening Edition, Wednesday, November 11, 2026
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington home to a U.S. military base after Iranian threats against his life, people familiar with the move told Reuters. The New York Times first reported the move; the base was not named. A Treasury spokesperson said Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade." A source said concerns grew because a published aerial photo let his Georgetown home be located. The Times said at least a half dozen top officials have moved to bases or secure housing over the past year. Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials on U.S. soil. The move follows Tuesday's federal indictment of three Iran-backed operatives over nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S.

U.S. stocks rose Wednesday as AI shares rebounded, with the S&P 500 up 1.3% and nearly back from last week's AI-driven sell-off. The Associated Press reported the S&P 500 rose 98.45 points to 7,619.38, within 2.6% of its October record. The Nasdaq rose 1.6% to 25,466.19 and the Dow rose 254.60 points, or 0.5%, to 52,486.49. CoreWeave led the gains after reporting stronger summer results than analysts expected. The bond market was closed for Veterans Day, and oil prices rose.

President Trump used his Veterans Day speech at Arlington National Cemetery to defend the Iran war, saying it will end "soon" with "total victory." "America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979," Trump said after laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. "We want to make sure we have a total victory. Not a 93% victory." He said "we lost 18 beautiful souls"; Pentagon casualty figures list 23 U.S. service members killed and at least 865 wounded in connection with the war. He also said his planned triumphal arch near the cemetery would be dedicated "soon." On Tuesday, nine Kennedy family members asked a federal court to block the arch, saying it would shadow President John F. Kennedy's grave.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, November 11, 2026
item.description:
The resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was sent to the House Judiciary Committee on a 211-204 vote, blocking a floor vote on removing him. The House voted Tuesday at 6:02 p.m. ET on a motion to refer Rep. Thomas Massie's resolution (H. Res. 1655) to committee: 210 Republicans and one independent voted yes; 203 Democrats and Massie, a Kentucky Republican, voted no; 18 members did not vote (7 Republicans, 11 Democrats), the House Clerk's roll call shows. The articles accused Hegseth over his conduct in office and his handling of the Iran war. The committee is not required to act, and Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.

Iran declared Argentina's navy and air force "terrorist organizations," in reply to Argentina's March listing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Iran's Foreign Ministry said it acted under a 2019 law allowing reciprocal steps against countries that back the U.S. designation of the Revolutionary Guard, and said Argentina would bear responsibility for the consequences; it named no specific measures. Argentina's government designated the Guard a terrorist group on March 31, citing the 1992 Israeli Embassy and 1994 AMIA bombings in Buenos Aires, which killed 29 and 85 people. Iran denies involvement.

Russia's Baltic oil port of Ust-Luga caught fire after a Ukrainian drone attack overnight, injuring three workers, the regional governor said. Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko said about 150 drones were shot down over the region and a transformer substation was shut down. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia warned of a drone threat, and Finland imposed temporary partial airspace and maritime curbs. In the Smolensk region, the governor said drone debris hit an apartment building in Yartsevo, killing two people. The strikes came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations began a second day of U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.

A minivan crashed into people outside a Los Angeles Metro station in North Hollywood at rush hour Tuesday, killing three, authorities said. The vehicle ended up under a food vendor's tent at the busy Lankershim and Chandler boulevards intersection just before 6 p.m. local time. The driver, a man in his 60s, and at least two others were critically injured. Police have not given a cause.

Jim Jordan will lead House Republicans in the minority after beating Steve Scalise 106-73, while Senate Republicans kept John Thune as their leader. Jordan, the Ohio Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee and co-founded the Freedom Caucus, won a secret-ballot vote of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress over Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana; Speaker Mike Johnson did not run. Tom Emmer of Minnesota beat August Pfluger of Texas for whip, the No. 2 minority post, and Lisa McClain of Michigan kept the conference chair job. In the Senate, Republicans first voted 31-15 to hold elections Tuesday rather than delay them, then re-elected Thune as leader, John Barrasso as whip and Tom Cotton as conference chair by acclamation. Both parties' leaders take their new minority roles when the new Congress convenes in January.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the effort to impeach him "a farce" in his first Pentagon news conference in six months, hours before a scheduled House vote. Hegseth said the operations cited in Rep. Thomas Massie's eight articles, including the Iran war, strikes on suspected drug boats and actions in Venezuela and Yemen, were lawful orders from the commander in chief and called the charges "partisan policy disagreements." The House scheduled a procedural vote for about 5:30 p.m. ET Tuesday on whether to block or refer the resolution; if that fails, Massie said he will seek a separate vote on each article. Removal would require a House impeachment and a two-thirds Senate vote; retiring Sen. Thom Tillis said he is "likely to vote against Hegseth" if a trial comes.

Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, after 0.6% in September, the Labor Department said; prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3%. Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for over 30% of the monthly increase; food rose 0.5% and energy 0.7%, with gasoline up 1.0%. Used cars and trucks and communication fell. Core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. BLS published no 12-month inflation rates because it collected no October 2025 data during the 2025 government shutdown. Separately, real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September, as hourly pay and prices both rose 0.4%.

Nvidia's independent directors hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate CEO Jensen Huang, as the stock fell again. The board said the probe will examine whether company secrets or national security were compromised after Huang told staff he had an affair with a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe worked for Chinese intelligence; she has not been charged. Nvidia shares closed down about 5.5% Tuesday at $168.89 after a 4.3% drop Monday, and Reuters reported Microsoft briefly passed Nvidia as the world's second-most valuable company, the first time since June 2025. Reuters said it could not verify a report by The Information on the woman's role in chip sales to China.

Three Iran-backed operatives were charged in Manhattan with roles in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S., including a plot against Britain's RAF Fairford. The eight-count superseding indictment unsealed Tuesday charges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism offenses in support of Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hizballah. Prosecutors allege al-Hassani orchestrated the September plot at RAF Fairford, which then housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel, and that al-Saadi, jailed in New York since his May arrest, passed coded messages through third parties to help coordinate it. Only al-Saadi is in custody. The charges are allegations.

A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile off Oman near the Strait of Hormuz, the British military's maritime agency UKMTO said; the crew is safe. UKMTO said the master of the tanker reported the hit at 1338 UTC (8:38 a.m. ET) Tuesday about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman. No environmental damage was reported, and the master will assess damage at first light. The tanker was not named and UKMTO did not say who fired. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed further attacks that have not been independently confirmed.

The U.N. review of the U.S. human rights record was postponed to January after the Trump administration skipped it for a second time. The U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva agreed to move the Universal Periodic Review of the United States to Jan. 18-29, 2027, after Washington did not attend Tuesday's rescheduled session. Every U.N. member state goes through the review about every four to five years.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, November 10, 2026
item.description:
The Iran war is "militarily effectively over," President Trump said Monday after meeting Qatar's prime minister, adding that renewed U.S. strikes are "quite unlikely." In a surprise White House briefing-room appearance, Trump said, "Iran militarily is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," and that Iran has been "decapitated," but he is still seeking a long-term solution to Iran's nuclear program. He said he saw "positive momentum" and a "good chance" the war could end, but "we're locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes." In a Truth Social post he said Gulf allies including Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE "would prefer the status quo." Trump gave no sign of a troop drawdown and said the naval blockade on Iranian oil continues: "We're keeping it going." Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, said they discussed "ways to progress the US-Iran talks." No deal has been announced.

U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine began Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, their first three-way meeting since February. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner lead the American side in the two-day talks; Ukraine's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov and Russia's by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky. Umerov said Kyiv's priorities are ending hostilities, reliable postwar security guarantees, economic recovery and humanitarian measures; Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said security issues would top the agenda. Moscow still demands Ukraine withdraw from four regions and abandon its NATO bid, which Kyiv rejects. Overnight, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile.

A bipartisan bill to speed permits for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects cleared its first Senate test vote Monday, 73-25. The Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, the vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, its first major action since the midterms; 51 Republicans, 21 Democrats and one independent voted yes. The 494-page bill, written by Sens. Martin Heinrich, Sheldon Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee, would limit how long lawsuits and reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act can run, protect already issued permits, expand federal power to site big interstate transmission lines and make data-center developers pay for grid upgrades they need. President Trump backs it; some environmental groups and the National Congress of American Indians oppose it, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is still reviewing it. Debate resumes at noon Tuesday with roll-call votes expected; the bill still needs final Senate passage and House approval.

The FBI is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese agent, President Trump said, adding Huang will be "in good shape." "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at Monday's White House briefing, calling Huang "a very honorable man" and saying Huang told him he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." China's foreign ministry called the spy allegation "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Huang has apologized for the affair and said he supports Nvidia's independent board investigation and will cooperate fully. Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen next week.

China's trade surplus topped $1 trillion for a second straight year, as October exports jumped 35% from a year earlier, customs data showed. China logged a $1.04 trillion surplus from January through October. October's surplus was $105.3 billion, down from $133.5 billion in September; imports also rose. Strong demand for high-tech goods such as computer chips and autos drove exports.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces a forced House impeachment vote after Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight articles Monday, mostly over the Iran war. Massie, a Kentucky Republican retiring at the end of the year, filed the resolution as privileged as the House returned Monday for its first session since the midterms, which requires House leaders to bring it to the floor within two legislative days, by Wednesday; Republicans can instead move to table it or refer it to committee by majority vote. Three articles charge waging the Iran war without a declaration, authorization or imminent threat, in violation of the War Powers Resolution; others cite ignoring civilian-casualty laws, the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific boat strikes, the capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro without congressional approval, strikes on Yemen, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly. A simple House majority would impeach; removal would need two-thirds of the Senate.

Stocks had their best day since April Monday, with the S&P 500 up 2.3%, as oil prices fell and Nvidia sank on its CEO probe. The S&P 500 rose to 7,549.94, the Dow gained 1,104 points (2.2%) to 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq climbed 2.7% to 25,253.14, recovering most of last week's midterm-driven selloff in AI stocks. Brent crude fell more than 5% to about $92.60 a barrel on hopes for Iran diplomacy. Nvidia fell 4.3% after its board opened an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Border wall construction in Texas's Big Bend region can resume after the Supreme Court paused a judge's order blocking it, 8-1. In an unsigned order in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, the court stayed U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone's Oct. 2 preliminary injunction while the case continues, saying the government is "exceedingly likely to prevail" that she lacked jurisdiction; the law lets courts hear only constitutional claims against the Homeland Security secretary's environmental-law waivers, and "there is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim." The court cited border security and costs of nearly $500,000 a day from the halt. It declined to summarily reverse. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have denied the stay. This is not a final ruling on the waivers.

DACA recipients could get permanent legal status through a bipartisan deal, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, but "amnesty is never going to be a solution." Mullin told reporters Monday that President Trump encouraged him to work with Democrats who had reached out, that no concrete policy changes have been discussed yet, and that any DACA fix is up to Congress. His comments followed Trump's Sunday 60 Minutes interview saying the deportation crackdown "might be too tough" and a deal on long-term immigrants is "doable."

Brett Shumate, head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, resigned Monday, the fourth senior DOJ official to leave since the midterms, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced. Shumate follows Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, National Security Division head John Eisenberg and Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones. Blanche credited the Civil Division with suits against sanctuary policies, settlements over corporate DEI practices, and closing clinics that provided gender-affirming care to minors. It was not clear whether the administration will seek Senate-confirmed replacements before Republicans lose Senate control in January.

Rocket Lab reported record third-quarter revenue of $268 million, up 73% from a year earlier, with its backlog up 52% to about $3.6 billion. The company posted a net loss of $79.7 million, or 12 cents a share, and its first positive GAAP operating cash flow of $7.2 million. It signed about $1 billion in new launch contracts, including more than $515 million for its Neutron rocket, whose first launch is now targeted for no earlier than 2027. Fourth-quarter revenue guidance is $270 million to $290 million.

DC Studios chiefs James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down after four years, Skydance said, naming former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham to lead it Dec. 1. Latcham, a founding member of the Marvel Cinematic Universe team, becomes president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. Gunn and Safran return to creative work, including Gunn's Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, due July 9, 2027, and The Batman Part II, now in production. Their 2025 Superman earned more than $618 million worldwide.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia's leading independent newspaper, closed its Moscow office Monday after three decades, citing state pressure. Authorities had labeled the paper a "foreign agent," ordered it out of its Moscow premises and barred Russian banks from processing reader donations. Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov said the constitution's guarantees of political and civil rights had "ceased to function"; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called it part of a "rotational process" in the media market. Six of its journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya, were killed since 1993.

item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, November 9, 2026
item.description:
Trump's deportation crackdown "might be too tough," the president said on 60 Minutes, adding a deal with Democrats on long-term immigrants is "doable." In the interview, taped Friday and aired Sunday on CBS, Trump said the crackdown "both helped and hurt" and that "we also took people that had good jobs." Asked whether the policy was too tough, he said, "I think it might be too tough, yeah." He described a possible deal that would deport "the killers," "the rough ones" and "the drug dealers" while letting people who have been "here for ten and 15 years" stay, said Democrats had "already called me," and acknowledged some in his administration want everyone removed. No bill, order or formal proposal exists. About an hour after the taping, per CBS, Trump named Stephen Miller, an immigration hardliner, White House chief of staff; Miller starts Monday. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said, "That's not a course correction. That's a promotion." Trump also said countries protected by U.S. escorts in the Strait of Hormuz "are going to pay us back any and all costs that we've had for the war," without giving a figure.

Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said Sunday a committee of independent directors, advised by outside independent counsel, will investigate the reporting; it said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," that it has confidence in Huang, and that he will remain CEO and cooperate. In an email to employees, Huang wrote, "I was unfaithful to my wife," apologized, and said, "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security." AP, citing The New York Times, said Huang had told the board of a relationship with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing. China's Foreign Ministry called the spying claim groundless. Nvidia shares fell about 4% to 5% in premarket trading Monday, CNBC reported. The company reports earnings Nov. 17.

U.S.-China trade truce measures were extended by both sides, with China keeping its extra 24% tariff on U.S. goods suspended for two more months. China's tariff commission said the 24% additional tariff stays suspended for two months from 1:01 p.m. Beijing time Tuesday, while a 10% extra tariff remains; its transport ministry extended the suspension of special port fees on U.S.-linked ships to Jan. 10, 2027, with its probe on hold. Beijing cited the consensus from the leaders' meeting in September. On the U.S. side, the trade representative extended the pause on Section 301 port fees for Chinese-linked ships and duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and cargo equipment through 11:59 p.m. ET Jan. 9, 2027, "to allow for further discussion with China," and the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security kept its "Affiliates Rule" export-control expansion on hold through Jan. 10, 2027 (Federal Register, Nov. 9).

Iraq's Khor Mor gas field stopped production after a suspected drone attack, knocking out power to most of the Kurdistan Region. Operator Dana Gas said production halted after a "suspected" drone attack late Sunday sparked a fire, which was put out; no staff were hurt. The Kurdistan Regional Government's electricity ministry said about 2,800 megawatts of generation went offline, and officials told Al Jazeera more than 70% of the region lost power, with hydro and alternative-fuel plants supplying hospitals and water stations. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered a joint investigation. No group claimed the attack; Kurdish officials have blamed earlier attacks on the field on Iran-backed militias.

Iran talks are not near a breakthrough, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, calling some Iranian demands "outrageous and ridiculous." Rubio said Sunday before leaving for the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris, "I wouldn't say we're at the verge of a breakthrough," and that Iran's demands were "not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's "2-day proposal stands": on day one the U.S. would end the war on all fronts, lift sanctions, reduce its regional presence and unfreeze assets, and on day two Iran would reopen Hormuz shipping; he said the alternative was war. Trump told CNN renewed strikes were "highly unlikely" if Iran signs "a very strong agreement," said the U.S. has identified targets including 38 bridges, and posted that "Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect." Trump meets Qatar's prime minister Monday. Separately, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Iraq reached understandings with the U.S. to let its oil exports pass through Hormuz via a lane near Oman, Reuters reported.

Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation into the Kraków shooting, and officials said four of the six people killed were Polish. The regional governor said the dead were four women and two men: three of the women and one man were Polish, one man was from the United Kingdom and one woman was from Austria. The wounded include citizens of Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The national prosecutor's office said it is investigating the killing of six people with a firearm and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński, who said Saturday the 24-year-old suspect was drawn to far-right ideologies, said Sunday that was one hypothesis police are checking and that officials are "not passing any verdicts." Police have not publicly named the suspect.

Gadi Eisenkot formally received the mandate to form Israel's next government Sunday, starting a 28-day clock to build a coalition of at least 61 seats. President Isaac Herzog handed the Yashar party leader the mandate at the President's Residence in Jerusalem, saying representatives of 67 incoming lawmakers recommended Eisenkot, against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog may grant up to 14 more days if needed. Eisenkot said Israel is in a state of emergency "approaching a point of no return," called for a "national emergency government" and urged Likud and Religious Zionism lawmakers to join a government under his leadership; Netanyahu has called for a unity government. Likud remains the largest party, and Eisenkot's bloc lacks a clear majority.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said Democratic lawmakers' threats against the administration could be criminal, but he did not announce an investigation or name a crime. Asked on CNN's "State of the Union" whether the Democratic rhetoric was a crime, Blanche said, "It depends on what's said. So yes, there could be," and added that he is not saying every case would be prosecuted. He said he would be "very worried" if he were on the House Oversight Committee, whose incoming chair, Rep. Robert Garcia, told Trump allies to "lawyer up," and that Justice Department lawyers will defend administration officials, including incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller, if oversight turns improper. He said, "I welcome oversight." Garcia has said Democrats "are not going to be intimidated." Saturday, Trump said he was ordering a Justice Department inquiry into Democrats' alleged threats; no investigation has been announced.

Treasury on Friday cut a major crypto exchange off from U.S. banks, saying it moved at least $16 billion in illicit funds, and sanctioned eight Canadian money businesses linked to Iran. FinCEN's order under section 9714 of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act bars U.S. financial institutions from transmitting funds to or from the exchange and takes effect 30 days after Federal Register publication. Treasury said the exchange moved at least $16 billion between May 2021 and May 2026 tied to Iranian, North Korean and Russian sanctions evasion and cybercrime, including about $22 million for Iran's central bank and the IRGC. It does not freeze user assets. Separately, OFAC designated eight Canadian money services businesses that convert Iranian rials into digital assets, some tied to IRGC-linked addresses and to sanctioned Canadian drug trafficker Ryan Wedding's laundering. Both actions were announced Friday as part of Operation Economic Outcast; the exchange has said operations are normal.

Poland began two days of national mourning Sunday, and police said the three people found dead at the Kraków gunman's home were his parents and sister. The 24-year-old suspect, who authorities say held far-right, ultranationalist views, is in critical condition in a hospital after police shot him during Saturday's attack, which killed six people and wounded 15 in the Old Town's Main Square. The family home is in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Kraków, where police said several firearms were seized; he and his father belonged to a shooting club. A British national was among the dead, and the wounded include citizens of Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police officers who stopped the attacker are hospitalized, one in critical condition. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it far-right terrorism; the square stayed partly sealed off Sunday.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński, who said Saturday the 24-year-old suspect was drawn to far-right ideologies, said Sunday that was one hypothesis police are checking and that officials are "not passing any verdicts." Police have not publicly named the suspect.

Gadi Eisenkot formally received the mandate to form Israel's next government Sunday, starting a 28-day clock to build a coalition of at least 61 seats. President Isaac Herzog handed the Yashar party leader the mandate at the President's Residence in Jerusalem, saying representatives of 67 incoming lawmakers recommended Eisenkot, against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog may grant up to 14 more days if needed. Eisenkot said Israel is in a state of emergency "approaching a point of no return," called for a "national emergency government" and urged Likud and Religious Zionism lawmakers to join a government under his leadership; Netanyahu has called for a unity government. Likud remains the largest party, and Eisenkot's bloc lacks a clear majority.

Treasury on Friday cut a major crypto exchange off from U.S. banks, saying it moved at least $16 billion in illicit funds, and sanctioned eight Canadian money businesses linked to Iran. FinCEN's order under section 9714 of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act bars U.S. financial institutions from transmitting funds to or from the exchange and takes effect 30 days after Federal Register publication. Treasury said the exchange moved at least $16 billion between May 2021 and May 2026 tied to Iranian, North Korean and Russian sanctions evasion and cybercrime, including about $22 million for Iran's central bank and the IRGC. It does not freeze user assets. Separately, OFAC designated eight Canadian money services businesses that convert Iranian rials into digital assets, some tied to IRGC-linked addresses and to sanctioned Canadian drug trafficker Ryan Wedding's laundering. Both actions were announced Friday as part of Operation Economic Outcast; the exchange has said operations are normal.

A sand cliff collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp in Gaza's Deir al-Balah after heavy rain, killing five people, including three children, Gaza's Civil Defense said. Rescuers recovered five bodies, including a woman and three children, and pulled five injured people out alive; the search for missing people continues. Gaza's government media office said about 70,000 tents were flooded or damaged in the storm that began Saturday.

A Nigerian court voided Atiku Abubakar's nomination as the opposition African Democratic Congress candidate for January's presidential election; the party said it will appeal. A Federal High Court judge in Abuja set aside the processes that produced the ADC's leadership and Atiku's nomination, after a former party official argued the officials were not chosen at a national convention. The ADC called the ruling a politically motivated attempt to weaken the opposition and said it would go to the Court of Appeal. Atiku, vice president from 1999 to 2007 and runner-up in the last election, won the ADC ticket in May. Ruling was Thursday; the election is Jan. 16.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, November 8, 2026
item.description:
Poland began two days of national mourning Sunday, and police said the three people found dead at the Kraków gunman's home were his parents and sister. The 24-year-old suspect, who authorities say held far-right, ultranationalist views, is in critical condition in a hospital after police shot him during Saturday's attack, which killed six people and wounded 15 in the Old Town's Main Square. The family home is in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Kraków, where police said several firearms were seized; he and his father belonged to a shooting club. A British national was among the dead, and the wounded include citizens of Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police officers who stopped the attacker are hospitalized, one in critical condition. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it far-right terrorism; the square stayed partly sealed off Sunday.

Saudi Aramco's tower in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris Sunday after Saudi air defenses intercepted missiles fired at the capital by Yemen's Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and later two cruise missiles and a drone over the Riyadh and southern regions; another missile aimed at the Eastern Province was also intercepted. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry called it an attempted attack on an Aramco administrative building and said shrapnel caused limited damage and no injuries; witnesses saw blown-out windows across several floors of the tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. Civil Defense alerts in Riyadh and other cities were lifted after the danger passed. The Houthis had not claimed the attack. It follows Saturday's airstrikes near Sanaa that the Houthi-run health ministry blamed on Saudi Arabia. Separately, the United Arab Emirates said it rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman.

Iran hanged three men Sunday over January's anti-government protests in Karaj, its judiciary said, accusing them of armed unrest and working for Israel and the U.S. The judiciary named the men as Hassan Divband (rendered Dioband by Reuters), Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh and said they used firearms, grenades and Molotov cocktails, set fire to public facilities and damaged an electricity substation, causing power outages. The Supreme Court upheld their death sentences and their assets were ordered confiscated; eight co-defendants received prison terms of five to 10 years. Rights groups have said protest cases relied on rushed trials and coerced confessions.

A gunman killed six people and wounded at least 15 in Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday; Poland's defense minister called it an act of terror. Police said the 25-year-old Polish suspect drove to several spots around the square in Kraków's Old Town shortly after 3 p.m. local time and opened fire with an automatic weapon at each stop before officers shot and wounded him; he is hospitalized after surgery. Four women and two men were killed; police said at least one victim was British. Two police officers were among the wounded. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideologies and held "ultranationalistic" views, and that he may have taken the weapons from his family's home, where his father held gun permits. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Saturday evening that two women and a man were found dead in the suspect's home and were likely close family members. Authorities said there is no indication of a second attacker.

President Trump said he is ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he called threats against Republicans. In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump said Democrats were "threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General," with impeachment and other punishment, called it "extortion at the highest level" and wrote, "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" He did not identify the "threatening letters" he cited, who sent them or who received them, and gave no evidence of a crime. He singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. The White House and Slotkin did not immediately comment, and the Justice Department has not announced an investigation.

The U.S. military disabled a cargo ship trying to break the Iran blockade and set up a new task force to choke Iran's land and Caspian routes. U.S. Central Command said a U.S. aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to leave the region following a call at an Iranian port; the crew had been told to leave the targeted spaces. CENTCOM said blockade enforcement since July has redirected 147 vessels and disabled five that refused to comply. Separately, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered the formation of Task Force Iron Gate, a staff of about 20 civilian and military personnel in Tampa that will work with other agencies to stop weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned goods and illicit revenue from moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM estimates the naval blockade has kept Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil. Also Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard spokesman said the country had lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit on missile range.

Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main challenger, will get the first chance to form Israel's next government, President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday. Herzog informed Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his decision Saturday evening and will formally hand Eisenkot the mandate at a ceremony Sunday. Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the Yashar party, was recommended by parties representing 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu. He has 28 days to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with a possible 14-day extension. His four-party bloc won 48 seats in the Oct. 27 election and Netanyahu's bloc 53. Earlier Saturday, Netanyahu called for a national unity government.

The Justice Department is joining Texas' $1.8 billion Medicaid-fraud lawsuit against Planned Parenthood, according to a court filing. The department said in a filing late Friday that it intends to intervene in the 2021 False Claims Act case in federal court in Amarillo, brought by outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and an anonymous whistleblower. The suit says Planned Parenthood kept billing Texas and Louisiana Medicaid after the states moved to cut it off and did not repay the money once the terminations took effect; the plaintiffs seek about $1.8 billion in repayments and penalties. Planned Parenthood says the billing was legal while courts had paused the terminations, has said a loss would force it to shut down in Texas, and said Saturday it will fight the case at trial, expected in 2027. The Justice Department under President Biden declined to join the case in 2021. The filing came days after Texans elected Democrat Nathan Johnson as the next attorney general.

Airstrikes on a village near Yemen's capital killed at least 27 people, mostly women and children, the Houthi-run health ministry said, blaming Saudi Arabia. A Sanaa hospital director said many victims, including first responders, remained under rubble. The toll could not be independently verified; Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment. It is one of the deadliest reported attacks since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July as a spillover of the U.S.-Iran conflict, shattering a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce.

UFC chief Dana White was offered the White House press secretary job, President Trump said Saturday; it is unclear whether White accepted. Trump wrote on Truth Social that White "has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States" and asked him to bring current and former UFC fighters as assistants. White then posted an image of himself behind the briefing-room lectern on Instagram with the caption "On to the next chapter." The White House and UFC did not immediately comment. The post has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left in October, five days after succeeding Karoline Leavitt. It follows Friday's announcement that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff.

A federal judge plans to appoint former U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu to investigate whether officials misled the court over Trump's East Potomac golf course project. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Saturday that Liu, who was D.C.'s top federal prosecutor in Trump's first term, would examine as special master whether Interior Department, National Park Service and Justice Department officials violated ethics rules or misled her about the renovation plans and the cutting of hundreds of trees. Both sides have until Friday, when the next hearing is set, to respond. The administration plans to close the public course Nov. 15 for a 15-month rebuild; Reyes' injunction bars further tree removal while the case continues.

item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, November 7, 2026
item.description:
President Trump said the U.S. carried out "minor" strikes Friday on an Iranian air-defense system, as Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island. Speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach on Friday evening, Trump said Iranians "built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." Iranian state media reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes are the first since Tuesday's midterms; the U.S. also carried out limited "defensive" strikes on Qeshm on Monday. Trump did not give further target details. CENTCOM said the situation was "relatively calm" and separately offered up to $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear program. Trump said mediators are still talking to Iran.

New Zealand's National Party narrowly leads Labour in preliminary election results, with the new Opportunity Party crossing 5% as a potential kingmaker. With most voting places reporting on election night (polls closed 7:00 p.m. NZDT / 1:00 a.m. ET Saturday), the Electoral Commission's preliminary count put National around 29.3% and Labour around 29.1%, projecting roughly 42 seats for National and 35 for Labour. Greens, ACT and New Zealand First remain in contention; the centrist Opportunity Party is on about 6% and about 7 seats, entering parliament for the first time. Special votes are still to come; official results are due Nov. 27. No government has been formed. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said the party is open to working with either major bloc and would talk first with the party that wins the most seats. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon had ruled out working with Opportunity before election night; National figures said it was too early to say.

The Justice Department voluntarily dropped its lawsuit seeking to segregate about 20,000 California mail ballots it said were cast by likely noncitizens. In a Rule 41(a)(1) notice filed Friday in U.S. v. California (C.D. Cal. No. 2:26-cv-12025), DOJ said the Supreme Court's Nov. 2 denial of emergency relief and the fact that the challenged ballots would already be commingled by a Nov. 13 hearing left no segregating relief available. California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced the dismissal the same day, saying the administration quit rather than face an evidentiary hearing on its list. The case is distinct from the Washington state TRO and earlier California emergency-denial cards; it closes the California suit.

OpenAI closed about $11 billion in new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar. Bloomberg said the $11 billion was an initial close; the broader round could reach about $20 billion in coming weeks, down from an earlier target near $30 billion at a higher valuation amid the AI-stock rout. Reuters, citing a source and investors, separately said SoftBank and MGX participated and that the valuation came down from about $1.5 trillion sought earlier. No company investor-relations release was posted. Separately, Bloomberg reported Microsoft is winding down a 2023 arrangement renting Oracle AI-cloud capacity after declining to renew, citing older-generation Nvidia chips that no longer met its specs; Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong.

Stephen Miller will become White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles after Republicans lost Congress. President Trump said Friday that Miller, the deputy chief of staff for policy and a longtime immigration hardliner, takes over Nov. 9. Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, submitted her resignation Thursday night and will move to the Trump Political Operation. The change comes after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterms.

U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate edged to 4.1%, the Labor Department reported. Nonfarm payrolls rose 165,000, well above the 48,000 average monthly gain over the prior 12 months. The unemployment rate changed little at 4.1% from 4.2% in September. August was revised up by 53,000 to +186,000 and September up by 31,000 to +60,000, a combined +84,000. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% to $38.00, up 3.1% over the year. Gains were led by professional and business services (+70,000), health care (+42,000) and transportation and warehousing (+25,000); manufacturing added 19,000. People working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million.

Japan's Nikkei fell 6% into a bear market and South Korea's Kospi fell 6% Friday, extending Wall Street's AI-driven selloff. The Nikkei 225 closed down 5.96% at 57,434.77 after falling as much as 7.09%, its first close below 60,000 since May and more than 20% under its June record of 72,831.73. The Kospi closed down 6.02% at 5,059.69; it plunged more than 8% at the open, which halted trading for 20 minutes, and SK hynix fell 10.44% and Samsung Electronics 6.35%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.3% and Australia's ASX 200 0.5%. Thursday on Wall Street the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, the Nasdaq 5.5% and the Philadelphia semiconductor index about 12%. Analysts quoted by Yonhap and the Japan Times tied the selling to fears that a Democratic Congress will slow AI data-center construction and tighten AI rules. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said it will cut the daily intraday borrowed short-sale limit to 3% of a stock's 30-day average volume from 30% and raise short-sale margin to 130%, effective Nov. 9, and stood ready to use the National Stabilization Fund after the Taiex fell about 4.5% Friday.

FinCEN ordered U.S. banks to cut off a major Seychelles crypto exchange over at least $16 billion in illicit flows, including to Iran and Russia. Under Operation Economic Outcast, the Section 9714(a) order bars U.S. financial institutions from processing funds transfers involving the Seychelles-incorporated convertible virtual currency exchanger named in Treasury's Nov. 6 release, effective 30 days after Federal Register publication. Treasury said the platform facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit finance from May 2021 to May 2026, including nearly $1.5 billion tied to Russian sanctions evasion and about $22 million linked to Iran's Central Bank and the IRGC-Qods Force. The same day, OFAC designated eight Canada-based money services businesses for enabling Iranian digital-asset channels.

A Wisconsin infant died of measles, the state's first measles death since 1990, amid a 431-case outbreak. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services said Nov. 5 that a coroner listed measles as the immediate cause of death for an infant tied to the southwestern Wisconsin outbreak and released no further personal details. As of Nov. 3 the state had 431 measles cases in 13 counties, the most in more than 35 years, with nine hospitalizations. DHS said it has delivered 2,000 MMR doses to local health departments since Aug. 1.

Treasury and the U.S. trade representative pressed China to fully implement Busan rare-earth and farm commitments. Secretary Scott Bessent and USTR Jamieson Greer spoke Friday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng about the bilateral economic relationship and the Busan arrangement. Bessent emphasized full and immediate implementation and said the United States will closely assess concrete results. Greer stressed agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals.

Record flash flooding submerged McCaysville, Ga., and Copperhill, Tenn., and crews rescued more than 80 people. Overnight storms dumped roughly 8 to 11 inches of rain; the Toccoa/Ocoee River at Copperhill crested at a record 18.05 feet. AP reported buildings submerged toward rooftops, more than 80 rescues across the twin towns, and continued debris, road damage, boil-water advisories and downtown restrictions Friday as waters receded.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, November 6, 2026
item.description:
Japan's Nikkei fell 6% into a bear market and South Korea's Kospi fell 6% Friday, extending Wall Street's AI-driven selloff. The Nikkei 225 closed down 5.96% at 57,434.77 after falling as much as 7.09%, its first close below 60,000 since May and more than 20% under its June record of 72,831.73. The Kospi closed down 6.02% at 5,059.69; it plunged more than 8% at the open, which halted trading for 20 minutes, and SK hynix fell 10.44% and Samsung Electronics 6.35%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.3% and Australia's ASX 200 0.5%. Thursday on Wall Street the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, the Nasdaq 5.5% and the Philadelphia semiconductor index about 12%. Analysts quoted by Yonhap and the Japan Times tied the selling to fears that a Democratic Congress will slow AI data-center construction and tighten AI rules.

A federal judge barred construction of President Trump's 250-foot arch for 14 days, shortly after a planning commission approved the project 8-4. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted the temporary restraining order sought by the District of Columbia and Virginia, blocking construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbing work, utility installation and road closures at Memorial Circle. In a 33-page opinion she found the project likely violates federal law, that construction threatens irreparable harm and that a halt is in the public interest. She was unpersuaded by recent administration declarations that the arch has national-security value, saying they appear nowhere in the planning documents. The government must notify contractors and report to the court by Nov. 9. The National Capital Planning Commission had voted 8-4 late Thursday after hearing from about 100 opponents; the Justice Department had said excavation could begin within days. The administration argues Congress authorized the arch when it approved the Potomac bridge more than a century ago.

A federal judge barred the Justice Department from demanding that Washington state set aside ballots on a list of about 400 suspected noncitizens. U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead in Seattle granted in part a 14-day temporary restraining order. It bars DOJ and Homeland Security from demanding that Washington officials set aside a registered voter's ballot because the name is on the federal list, and from threatening officials with prosecution for counting ballots as state law requires. Prosecutors sent the list Oct. 26; the judge noted Washington found it included citizens who had already shown proof of citizenship, and that nothing in the record shows anyone on it was charged. Relying on the Ninth Circuit's United States v. California, he wrote that the government "did not ask" but directed the state. The order is narrow: it does not stop DOJ from investigating or prosecuting anyone who votes unlawfully, sharing information, or asking for cooperation. A hearing on a longer injunction is set for Nov. 18.

Paraguay's Congress refused to accept President Santiago Peña's resignation and opened an impeachment trial over the collapse of Ueno Bank. The central bank took over Ueno Bank on Tuesday after finding a severe capital shortfall; the lender says it has more than 3 million customers in a country of about 6.4 million and held roughly $800 million or more in public funds. Peña, who owned shares in the bank's controlling group until last year, announced his resignation by video just as the Chamber of Deputies unanimously approved impeachment. Colorado Party deputies then left a joint session, leaving it without a quorum, so the resignation was not accepted; opposition lawmakers said accepting it would make him a senator for life with legal protections. The Senate opened the trial Thursday night and summoned Peña to present his defense Friday at 10 a.m. local time. Removal needs 30 of 45 senators, and Vice President Pedro Alliana would take over. The attorney general ordered criminal investigations, and Peña says he will cooperate.

President Trump said he will decide "soon" whether to resume large-scale strikes on Iran after meeting his national security advisers; no order has been given. Asked after the meeting, Trump said: "Now we will make a decision... I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough." Axios, citing U.S. officials, reports he is weighing new strikes, continued economic pressure, or a deal with concessions to Iran, and that U.S. Central Command is finalizing preparations but has received no new directive. Qatari mediators are discussing a two-day confidence-building proposal under which the U.S. would lift its naval blockade and release some frozen funds, Iran would invite IAEA inspectors, and the Strait of Hormuz would then reopen. Iran's Mohsen Rezaei said in Moscow that Iran will not reopen the strait or negotiate until the U.S. meets seven conditions. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group will not reach the region before mid-November.

The Nasdaq composite fell 5.5% Thursday to 24,315, closing in a correction more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, as AI and chip stocks sold off. The S&P 500 fell 4.4%, or about 335 points, to 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025. The Dow Jones industrial average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, to 51,523.06, wiping out Wednesday's post-election rally. Nvidia fell about 9%; the Philadelphia semiconductor index plunged about 11%. Investors weighed weak chip outlooks, including Qualcomm's, and concern that Democratic wins in Congress and in states such as Texas could slow data-center buildout. The Nasdaq's Oct. 6 record close was 27,599.79.

Harmeet Dhillon resigned as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday. Blanche said he accepted her resignation after about 18 months in the post. Dhillon said she had told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles weeks earlier that she planned to leave after the midterms and would return to private practice. She was the first senior Justice Department official to exit after Democrats won Congress on Tuesday. Under Dhillon the division overhauled priorities, pursued university and voter-roll cases, and saw a large share of career lawyers leave.

The Justice Department is pursuing a criminal investigation into the 2022 Supreme Court abortion-ruling leak, The New York Times reported; DOJ declined to comment. The Times, citing people familiar with the inquiry, reports that prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court when the draft Dobbs opinion reached Politico in May 2022. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro in Washington is overseeing the probe and assigned prosecutor Carlton Davis. It is unclear what law prosecutors believe was broken or whether they have new evidence; some possibly relevant laws have five-year limits that would expire in the spring. Fox News, citing its own sources, says the probe has run at least a year and that it is unclear who received subpoenas. The Justice Department and the U.S. attorney's office declined to comment, and the court's spokeswoman did not respond. The court's own 2023 investigation did not identify the leaker.

A majority of 67 Israeli lawmakers backed Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister and 46 backed Netanyahu; President Herzog will name his pick Sunday. Herzog finished two days of consultations Thursday and said that, although the result appears clear, he must judge who can actually form a government, citing "mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs." He will hold personal talks with party leaders over the weekend and announce the mandate Sunday, Nov. 8. Eisenkot's Yashar party and five others recommended him, including both Arab-led parties, though Eisenkot has ruled out sitting with them; United Torah Judaism recommended no one. Netanyahu's Likud, with 27 seats, leads a bloc that won 53. The chosen candidate gets 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension; Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister meanwhile.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will change all 548 death sentences in the state to life in prison without parole. His office says the action applies to every person under sentence of death (529 men and 19 women), releases no one, grants no parole eligibility and leaves convictions and restitution orders in place. Because the California Constitution requires the state Supreme Court to review clemency for people twice convicted of felonies, his request has gone to the court; The Marshall Project reports that covers more than half of those affected and that, if approved, it would be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history. California's last execution was in 2006, and Newsom imposed an execution moratorium in 2019. His term ends in January.

item.title: Evening Edition, Thursday, November 5, 2026
item.description:
The Nasdaq composite fell 5.5% Thursday to 24,315, closing in a correction more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, as AI and chip stocks sold off. The S&P 500 fell 4.4%, or about 335 points, to 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025. The Dow Jones industrial average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, to 51,523.06, wiping out Wednesday's post-election rally. Nvidia fell about 9%; the Philadelphia semiconductor index plunged about 11%. Investors weighed weak chip outlooks, including Qualcomm's, and concern that Democratic wins in Congress and in states such as Texas could slow data-center buildout. The Nasdaq's Oct. 6 record close was 27,599.79.

Harmeet Dhillon resigned as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday. Blanche said he accepted her resignation after about 18 months in the post. Dhillon said she had told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles weeks earlier that she planned to leave after the midterms and would return to private practice. She was the first senior Justice Department official to exit after Democrats won Congress on Tuesday. Under Dhillon the division overhauled priorities, pursued university and voter-roll cases, and saw a large share of career lawyers leave.

A New York federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from deporting detained Afghans to Afghanistan or Pakistan through Saturday. U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni ordered the government to honor ICE's statement that it had no planned or confirmed charter or commercial flights for those removals through Nov. 7. Rights groups and dozens of lawmakers had warned of a Louisiana charter flight of about 150 Afghans via Pakistan. ICE said no such flights were planned or confirmed this week. The order does not decide the case's merits.

The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% from 3.75%, its first increase since August 2023, citing energy-driven inflation from the Middle East war. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 for a quarter-point hike; Catherine L. Mann favored 4.25%. UK CPI was 3.5% in September and is projected to reach about 5% by mid-2027. Governor Andrew Bailey said the move should not be seen as the start of an inevitable long sequence of hikes, but that another increase is likely unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. The next decision is Dec. 17.

Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass to become the next mayor of Los Angeles, and Bass conceded Thursday. AP projected Raman the winner. Returns showed Raman with about 52% to Bass's 48%. Raman, a City Council member, will take office in December. The race was part of Tuesday's midterm balloting.

Russell Brand was convicted in London of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women; sentencing is Monday. A Southwark Crown Court jury found Brand, 51, guilty after a four-week trial of offenses from 2004 to 2009. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one attempted indecent assault. The Crown Prosecution Service said he used his celebrity status to commit the crimes. He was remanded in custody; the judge said a significant custodial term is inevitable. Sentencing is Nov. 9.

Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 last week, the fewest since mid-July, and third-quarter productivity rose at a 3.6% annual rate. The Labor Department said claims for the week ended Oct. 31 dropped 6,000 from a revised 195,000; the four-week average was 194,750. Separately, BLS said nonfarm productivity rose 3.6% as output grew 3.7% and hours 0.1%, and unit labor costs fell 0.7%, the first decline in more than a year. The October jobs report is due Friday.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, November 5, 2026
item.description:
Rep. Thomas Massie says he will force a House vote next week to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and other military actions. Massie's eight articles of impeachment say the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution and that Hegseth ignored civilian-casualty laws. They also cite drug-boat strikes that killed at least 221 people, retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, the seizure of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores, and an unauthorized war in Yemen. Massie told CNN he will trigger the vote when Congress returns. He said he would drop the effort if Hegseth resigns. As a privileged resolution, it must get floor action within two legislative days, though the House could vote to table it. President Trump said Hegseth is "doing a very good job." A Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth "will not back down."

Two projectiles struck a tanker off northern Qatar overnight, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers and a tug caught fire near Hormuz. The British military's UKMTO said the tanker was hit about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, at 2320 UTC Wednesday. The crew's condition and the extent of the damage were not confirmed. Separately, the IRGC said one tanker hit a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz. It said a supertanker leaving the strait caught fire, and a tug helping it also caught fire. The IRGC said the ships had tried to use unauthorized routes. Qatar is mediating between the U.S. and Iran. A Qatari LNG carrier was hit on Oct. 30.

Medicare finalized its 2027 doctor-pay rule, cutting the basic payment rate about 2% as a one-year 2.5% boost expires. The conversion factor for doctors who do not qualify under alternative payment models drops 2.31%, to $32.63. For doctors who qualify, it drops 1.83%, to $32.95. When an office visit and a minor same-day procedure are billed together, the lower-cost service will be paid at 80%. Starting April 1, 2027, approved ACOs may reduce or waive Part B cost-sharing for many services. The rule also writes into regulation the new law limiting Medicare eligibility to citizens, green-card holders and a few other groups. The rule takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. CMS also finalized its 2027 hospital outpatient and home health payment rules.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to a French military air base Thursday after a bomb threat and landed safely. France's prime minister's office said the Airbus A320 landed at the Evreux base in Normandy. The French air force said it sent jets to escort the plane. Earlier this week, hoax threats against LOT, SAS, Wizz Air and Ryanair flights forced diversions.

Congress will be controlled by Democrats in January after they won both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, AP projected. AP called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday. Democrats flipped at least seven Republican-held Senate seats: Kansas (Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall, the state's first Democratic senator since 1932), Iowa (Josh Turek over Rep. Ashley Hinson), Texas (James Talarico over Ken Paxton), Ohio (Sherrod Brown over Sen. Jon Husted), Maine (Troy Jackson over Sen. Susan Collins), North Carolina (Roy Cooper) and South Carolina (Annie Andrews). They held Georgia (Sen. Jon Ossoff), Michigan (Abdul El-Sayed) and New Hampshire (Chris Pappas). In the House they flipped more than two dozen districts. As of 4 a.m. Eastern, Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi were still uncalled. Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black House speaker. Trump wrote that he "wasn't on the Ballot," vowed to veto Democratic bills and told Fox News he would accept the results; Senate Majority Leader John Thune vowed to resist the new majority's agenda. The new Congress is sworn in in January.

Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to lead House Republicans in the new Congress, setting up a race between Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan. Johnson told staff on a Wednesday morning call and wrote colleagues that the job's demands on his family drove the decision; he is expected to stay in the House as a rank-and-file member from Louisiana, AP reported, citing two people familiar with his decision. Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan each announced bids in letters to colleagues. House Republicans plan to elect their leaders Tuesday, Nov. 10, when Democrats will take the majority in January after Tuesday's midterms.

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 1,569 points, or 3%, Wednesday, its best day since April 2025, after Democrats won Congress, as oil prices fell. The Dow closed at 53,356.12; the S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,688.62 and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4% to 25,736.51. U.S. crude oil fell more than 7% after Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for Republican losses, and Treasury yields fell. Bank and retail stocks led; Nvidia, CoreWeave and Tesla fell amid concern over limits on data centers after Democrats' wins, including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's pledged moratorium.

The death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid site in Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, rose to 40 Wednesday, with more than 30 people possibly still under rubble, Zelenskyy said. Rescuers have searched for three days after Monday's strikes on a school used to hand out aid and a nearby shelter in the Zaporizhzhia region village. AP called it one of the deadliest strikes in the region in nearly five years of full-scale war; Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted Ukrainian military units. Russian attacks also caused hours of power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions Wednesday, AP reported.

Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms, writing, "The reason we lost is the war." In a long post Wednesday, Vance said many 2024 Trump voters backed Democrats to end the war, over the cost of living, to put America first and to change the U.S. relationship with Israel, and called a suggestion to seek a diplomatic resolution with Iran "sound." Asked about it, President Trump said he agreed the war "drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term" but said he would do it again because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon (Axios, Reuters). Trump also told reporters he is not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying "No, I think he's doing a very good job," after CBS News reported, citing multiple sources, that he had asked advisers whether Hegseth should stay.

Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remained too close to call Wednesday, with Democrats leading both by fewer than 700 votes. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 65 votes out of about 925,000 with 96% of the expected vote counted; mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive through Nov. 10, the state has no formal recount process, and certification is due Nov. 13 (Mississippi secretary of state's office via ABC News). In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan 48.2% to 47.9%, by 626 votes, with 74% counted; if no one reaches 50%, ranked-choice tabulation begins Nov. 18. Democrats have already secured 54 Senate seats. AP said 59 House races where party control is at stake were also uncalled as of 4 p.m. Eastern.

A gunman killed a woman at Citibank's Brandon, Fla., office campus near Tampa Wednesday before a Citibank security guard shot him dead, the sheriff's office said. The driver crashed a sedan through a fence into an outdoor dining area at about 12:11 p.m., shot a woman eating lunch, then went inside toward the cafeteria, where an armed security officer exchanged fire with him, Hillsborough County Chief Deputy Frank Losat said; the gunman died at Tampa General Hospital. Four other people had non-life-threatening injuries. Sheriff Chad Chronister called it a targeted incident. About 3,200 employees were on the campus; 367 deputies and federal agents responded. Names and a motive were not released.

Private employers added 86,000 jobs in October, matching September's revised gain, payroll processor ADP said Wednesday. Trade, transportation and utilities added 39,000, education and health services 28,000 and leisure and hospitality 19,000, while professional and business services lost 27,000. Pay for workers who stayed in their jobs rose 3.2% from a year earlier. Separately, the Institute for Supply Management's services index slipped to 54.5 in October from 54.9, its 28th straight month of growth. The government's October jobs report is due Friday.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, November 4, 2026
item.description:

AP called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday. Democrats flipped at least seven Republican-held Senate seats: Kansas (Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall, the state's first Democratic senator since 1932), Iowa (Josh Turek over Rep. Ashley Hinson), Texas (James Talarico over Ken Paxton), Ohio (Sherrod Brown over Sen. Trump wrote that he "wasn't on the Ballot," vowed to veto Democratic bills and told Fox News he would accept the results; Senate Majority Leader John Thune vowed to resist the new majority's agenda. The new Congress is sworn in in January.

Governors' offices in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Iowa flipped to Democrats Tuesday, giving the party a majority of governorships for the first time since 2006, AP reported. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa ousted third-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat elected statewide there since 1994. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any U.S. state. Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, and Rob Sand beat Zach Lahn in Iowa. Republicans held Florida, where Byron Donalds became the nation's first Black Republican elected governor. Democratic Govs. Kathy Hochul (N.Y.), Josh Shapiro (Pa.), JB Pritzker (Ill.), Wes Moore (Md.), Maura Healey (Mass.) and Tina Kotek (Ore.) won reelection, and Xavier Becerra won California. Thirty-six states elected governors.

Abortion-rights measures won in Missouri, Virginia and Nevada on Tuesday, and Missouri voters rejected the state's 2025 Republican congressional map, AP reported. Missouri voters defeated an amendment that would have reimposed most abortion restrictions. Virginia added a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" to its constitution, covering abortion through the first two trimesters, and Nevada gave final approval to a right to abortion until fetal viability. Idaho voters rejected an abortion-rights measure. Maryland approved an amendment paving the way for new congressional districts in 2028. Florida approved a property tax break that triples the $50,000 homestead exemption for non-school taxes next year and raises it to $250,000 in 2028. California and Colorado rejected voter ID measures; Ohio, North Carolina and Nevada approved them. Nebraska and Arizona passed transgender restrictions. Voters decided 145 questions in more than three dozen states.

Two Spokane County, Wash., SWAT deputies were critically wounded and three people died, including the gunman, after a domestic violence call Tuesday near Spangle. The call came in around 2:25 p.m. Pacific time, Sheriff John Nowels said. A woman was also wounded, with injuries that are not life-threatening.

U.S. aid to Israel of about $4 billion a year will end after this year, President Trump said Tuesday, adding that Israel can still buy American weapons. In a phone interview with Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends" on Election Day, Trump said he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to it months ago, that Netanyahu proposed it, and that the U.S. would "help Israel if they need it." He did not say how the cutoff would work. The current 2016 memorandum of understanding provides $3.8 billion a year ($3.3 billion in military financing and $500 million for missile defense) through 2028, and the money is appropriated by Congress. Netanyahu's office declined to comment Tuesday.

Election Day voting ran with relatively few problems, AP reported, though ballot scanners failed across Westchester County, N.Y., and Florida moved 21 polling sites after flooding. In Westchester, scanners rejected ballots from poll opening after what officials described as a programming update; voters filled out paper ballots placed in sealed emergency bags, which officials said will be counted after polls close at 9 p.m. In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis's Executive Order 26-227 declared emergencies in seven counties, and the state Division of Elections listed temporary sites for 30 precincts in eight counties, including Brevard, Broward and Palm Beach.

Greenland's parliament approved a defense agreement with the U.S. and Denmark on Tuesday that opens the way for more American military bases on the island. The vote was 16-0 with seven abstentions. The deal, signed in September by President Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen at the U.N. General Assembly, lets the U.S. modernize and expand Pituffik Space Base. Greenland stays under Danish control, and the agreement would still apply if it becomes independent. It takes effect only after Denmark's parliament approves it; Danish lawmakers debate it later this month. No U.S. Senate approval is required.

Guam's governor's office goes to Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo, and Democrat Alicia Limtiaco unseated Del. James Moylan, final unofficial results show. Guam Election Commission unofficial results gave Ada-Calvo 15,945 votes (51.45%) to 14,925 for Democrats Therese Terlaje and Sabina Perez; Terlaje conceded. Limtiaco led Moylan, a Republican, 15,645 (51%) to 14,983 for Guam's non-voting seat in the U.S. House. Guam votes about 15 hours ahead of the East Coast, so these are the first 2026 midterm results. Results are unofficial until certified; off-island absentee ballots are counted Nov. 19.

The Justice Department may again warn election officials they risk prosecution for counting flagged ballots, after the full Ninth Circuit reinstated a stay Tuesday morning. In SEIU v. Department of Justice (No. 26-7303), a 2-1 panel on Monday stayed a San Francisco judge's order that barred DOJ from demanding that officials set aside ballots of voters it calls likely noncitizens and from warning of prosecution. A majority of active judges vacated that stay overnight and took the case en banc; on Election Day morning the en banc court reinstated the stay. Chief Judge Mary Murguia, joined by Judges Gould, Owens, H.A. Thomas and Desai, dissented. The district court's temporary restraining order would otherwise run through Nov. 16. Separately, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington late Monday barred DOJ and Homeland Security from sending states lists of suspected noncitizen voters or asking them to separate those ballots, in a Privacy Act case (Reuters).
