Ukraine's power grid was hit by Russia's largest attack on its energy system this year, cutting power and water in Kyiv ahead of U.S.-brokered talks set for Nov. 10-11. Ukraine said Russia launched 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles overnight, hitting energy sites in 10 regions; damage to a Kyiv regional power hub forced emergency blackouts along with water and public-transit outages. Private energy company DTEK said three of its five thermal plants stopped generating. U.S., Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are due to meet again in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.

A tanker was hit by two unidentified projectiles in its engine room about 14 nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman, Tuesday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations center said. UKMTO said the strike happened at 1900 GMT (2 p.m. ET) near the Strait of Hormuz, with no casualties or environmental damage reported, and advised ships to transit with caution.

Perpetual futures on individual U.S. stocks can begin trading on CFTC-registered exchanges, Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig said Tuesday. Selig's statement treats the contracts, which have no expiration date, as security futures under joint CFTC and SEC oversight, open to exchanges also notice-registered with the SEC to trade security futures. Perpetual futures have been widely traded in crypto markets offshore; Kalshi has filed listing standards for security futures with the SEC.

Job openings were little changed at 7.5 million in September, the Labor Department said Tuesday, while the number of people quitting jobs rose to 3.4 million. The openings rate was 4.5%. Hires were 5.4 million, total separations 5.3 million and layoffs and discharges 1.6 million. August openings were revised up 111,000 to 7.2 million.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, November 3, 2026
item.description:
Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz was hit Monday by limited U.S. "defensive" strikes on surface-to-air missiles used against U.S. aircraft, U.S. officials said. A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the strikes targeted "Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets"; Iranian state TV reported explosions on the island. The strikes appeared limited rather than a return to full hostilities, AP reported, and came on the eve of the midterms after President Trump had said the U.S. would not launch new strikes before them. The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes. The administration was last known to have attacked in early September; a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian oil continues and a third aircraft carrier is heading to the region. Hours earlier, Vice President JD Vance said he and Trump "feel pretty good" about a possible negotiated settlement; Qatari mediators held two rounds of talks with Iran last week.

California's mail ballots from about 20,000 people the government flagged as likely noncitizens will not be set aside, after the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration's emergency request Monday. The Court's brief order denied the Justice Department's application (No. 26A624) for an injunction pending appeal, without explanation and with no noted dissents, after a district court and a divided Ninth Circuit panel had refused. Also Monday, Chief Judge James Boasberg in Washington barred the Justice Department and Homeland Security from demanding that California election officials segregate ballots based on the federal lists, writing that the executive branch "has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause." California says the federal list is unreliable and includes many citizens.

The death toll from Russia's bombing of a humanitarian aid site in Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, rose to 31 Tuesday, with nearly 50 people still missing, the regional governor said. Russian bunker-busting bombs hit a school used to hand out aid in the Zaporizhzhia region village on Monday, then a shelter where residents had taken cover; the dead include four police officers and two rescue workers, acting regional head Mykhailo Semikin said, calling it one of the region's worst civilian tolls of the full-scale war. Three days of mourning were declared. Overnight, Russia fired 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, targeting power plants and forcing emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said; at least 62 people were wounded in the Kharkiv region and one was killed in the Dnipro area. Russia said it shot down 856 Ukrainian drones, and a Ukrainian drone damaged an oil refinery in Yaroslavl.

Australia's central bank raised its key interest rate a quarter point to 4.85% Tuesday, saying inflation is broadly based and now expected to stay high longer. The Reserve Bank of Australia's board voted 6-3 for the increase; three members wanted to hold at 4.60%. Its statement said inflation is partly driven by higher fuel and commodity prices tied to the Middle East conflict and by AI-related demand for technology goods, and is not expected to reach the top of its 2-3% target until late 2027, about three quarters later than forecast. It said the economy is slowing, home prices have fallen significantly and unemployment has risen. The bank posted no other releases with the decision.

The Justice Department's lawsuit demanding Harvard's applicant-level admissions records was dismissed Monday by a federal judge in Boston, who said the government skipped required steps. U.S. District Judge Myong Joun found the department had not taken required steps before suing: "the agency must advise the recipient of its failure to comply and determine that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means," he wrote. He said the ruling does not decide whether Harvard has discriminated, whether agencies may lawfully seek applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately have to provide it. The department, which began a compliance review in 2025, had sought five years of admissions data, including race, grades, test scores and essays, to check whether Harvard still considers race after the Supreme Court's 2023 ban on affirmative action.

The false-statements case against two former FBI officials over the Hunter Biden laptop was dismissed Monday by a federal magistrate judge who called it "weaponization." Ruling from the bench for about an hour, U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the District of Columbia found no probable cause on any element of the charge that Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023. The Justice Department said it "disagrees" and is "evaluating all options"; it could appeal to the chief judge or seek a grand jury indictment.

A business jet that crashed into a Greenacres, Fla., neighborhood Sunday, killing all nine aboard, went into a steep dive after its pilots reported icing and turbulence. The Learjet 60, flying from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas, crashed near a busy Palm Beach County roadway at 12:50 p.m. Sunday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, calling it a "horrific tragedy." Cruising east at 35,000 feet, the pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and asked to climb 2,000 feet; moments later the jet dove at up to 30,000 feet per minute, beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data reported by AP. A pilot declared an emergency before impact. Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone hurt on the ground. About 600 residents of a nearby mobile home community were evacuated. The victims have not been identified. The NTSB leads the investigation with FAA support and scheduled a media briefing Monday in West Palm Beach.

Charges against 63 people for illegal voting and related election crimes were announced by the Justice Department on Monday, the eve of the midterms. The cases, in federal districts from North Carolina and California to Tennessee, Pennsylvania and Nevada, include noncitizens accused of voting in federal elections, false claims of U.S. citizenship to register or vote, and one fraudulent out-of-state voter registration; the department says four are in the country illegally and most others are lawful permanent residents. Most alleged votes date to the 2022 and 2024 elections. Attorney General Todd Blanche called it "the largest surge of voter-fraud arrests" since Trump returned to office; the department says it has charged 239 people with voting-fraud-related offenses under this administration. Charges are accusations; defendants are presumed innocent.

Oak Creek in Sedona, Ariz., rose from about 3 feet to nearly 18 feet in what officials called unprecedented flooding, forcing more than 100 homes to evacuate. Oak Creek's flow hit about 20,000 cubic feet per second Sunday evening, about 100 times normal; evacuation orders also covered Camp Verde, Cottonwood, Rimrock and Winslow, Gila County ordered all of Gisela evacuated, and state police made rooftop helicopter rescues. No deaths were reported. In Florida, the National Weather Service declared a flash flood emergency Monday morning for Palm Bay, Melbourne and West Melbourne after 12 to 15 inches of rain, closing Brevard County schools.

Lumentum is being bought by Marvell in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion, one of the largest tech acquisitions ever, the companies said Monday. Lumentum holders would get 4.5 Marvell shares for each share, and Marvell holders would own about 67% of the combined company, which targets AI data-center connections. The deal needs shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first half of 2028.

The Justice Department said it "disagrees" and is "evaluating all options"; it could appeal to the chief judge or seek a grand jury indictment.

California's mail ballots from about 20,000 people the government suspects are noncitizens are now before the Supreme Court, after the Trump administration asked it Monday to order them set aside. Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed an emergency application (No. 26A624), submitted to Justice Elena Kagan, seeking an injunction pending appeal and an immediate administrative order, after a district court and a divided Ninth Circuit panel refused. California says the federal list is unreliable and includes many citizens. The Court set no deadline and had not acted by Monday evening; Election Day is Tuesday.

Oak Creek in Sedona, Ariz., rose from about 3 feet to nearly 18 feet in what officials called unprecedented flooding, forcing more than 100 homes to evacuate. Oak Creek's flow hit about 20,000 cubic feet per second Sunday evening, about 100 times normal; evacuation orders also covered Camp Verde, Cottonwood, Rimrock and Winslow, Gila County ordered all of Gisela evacuated, and state police made rooftop helicopter rescues. No deaths were reported. In Florida, the National Weather Service declared a flash flood emergency Monday morning for Palm Bay, Melbourne and West Melbourne after 12 to 15 inches of rain, closing Brevard County schools.

Lumentum is being bought by Marvell in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion, one of the largest tech acquisitions ever, the companies said Monday. Lumentum holders would get 4.5 Marvell shares for each share, and Marvell holders would own about 67% of the combined company, which targets AI data-center connections. The deal needs shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first half of 2028.

Apple's revenue rose 12% to a September-quarter record of $114.5 billion in CEO John Ternus' first earnings report, the company said Monday. Net income was $30.7 billion, or $2.10 a share, including about 5 cents from tariff refunds. iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion and services revenue a record $31.6 billion. Fiscal 2026 revenue was a record $479 billion. Revenue beat analysts' $113.4 billion estimate (LSEG, via CNBC).

The Learjet that crashed in Greenacres, Fla., may have started breaking apart in midair, the NTSB said Monday, after its crew reported icing at about 35,000 feet. The crew of the Learjet 60 reported light clear icing, moderate turbulence and precipitation before a rapid descent and a mayday call, investigators said; weather at cruise altitude is a focus. All nine aboard died Sunday and one person on the ground was hurt.

U.S. factory activity grew for a 10th straight month in October as the ISM manufacturing index rose to 55.5 from 54.5. Production rose to 59.0, its highest since November 2021; new orders were 55.5, employment 52.4 and prices 75.2, down from 77.9. Readings above 50 signal growth. Stocks closed mixed: the Dow rose 0.6% while the S&P 500 fell 0.3% and the Nasdaq 0.7% on a chip-stock slide, as oil fell on Iran deal hopes.

Government emergency apps in Ukraine and Russia sent fake nuclear and chemical alerts after hackers broke in, officials in both countries said Monday. Ukraine's Air Alert app pushed false alerts late Sunday; the air force said "There is no radiation threat," and the app was suspended and restored. Russia's emergencies ministry called its incident early Monday a "massive cyberattack" and said the public warning system itself was not affected. It is unclear whether the attacks are linked.

item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, November 2, 2026
item.description:
A business jet that crashed into a Greenacres, Fla., neighborhood Sunday, killing all nine aboard, went into a steep dive after its pilots reported icing and turbulence. The Learjet 60, flying from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas, crashed near a busy Palm Beach County roadway at 12:50 p.m. Sunday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, calling it a "horrific tragedy." Cruising east at 35,000 feet, the pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and asked to climb 2,000 feet; moments later the jet dove at up to 30,000 feet per minute, beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data reported by AP. A pilot declared an emergency before impact. Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone hurt on the ground. About 600 residents of a nearby mobile home community were evacuated. The victims have not been identified. The NTSB leads the investigation with FAA support and scheduled a media briefing Monday in West Palm Beach.

The Justice Department appealed the dismissal of its Alaska Senate lawsuit, as FBI agents questioned donors to Dan J. Sullivan, the candidate sharing Sen. Dan Sullivan's name. A federal judge dismissed the department's suit, which sought to block certification of the race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, on Sunday, and the department quickly appealed. FBI agents interviewed donors in Petersburg, Alaska, on Friday and Saturday as federal authorities expanded a monthslong criminal probe into allegations that Democratic campaigners recruited candidates to run against the senator; donors said agents asked whether they had felt deceived or meant to give to the senator, and one said agents cited possible "campaign finance" violations. Dan J. Sullivan's campaign raised $7,150, mostly from Petersburg. He has said he entered the race on his own and had no contact with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign; Peltola denies any role. No charges have been filed. Tuesday's race could decide Senate control.

Oil fell about 4% early Monday, pushing U.S. crude below $100 a barrel, on hopes that Qatar-mediated talks could end the Iran war. Brent crude for January fell 3.9% to $109.00 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate for December fell 4.1% to $99.85 as of 4:07 a.m. ET. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that President Trump has not made a decision and would "prefer to do it peacefully." Brent ended October at a six-month high on concern fighting could resume after Tuesday's midterms. OPEC+ kept December output targets unchanged on Sunday.

Russia resumed attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region after the six-day Oleshky truce expired Sunday night, and Kyiv said Russian forces used the pause to reinforce. The truce, brokered through first lady Melania Trump with Pope Leo's involvement, began Oct. 27 and expired at 2100 GMT (4 p.m. ET) Sunday after Moscow refused an extension, Ukrainian officials said; nearly 800 people were evacuated. Ukraine's General Staff said Russia rotated units, fortified positions and delivered ammunition during the pause; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggested Ukraine had also regrouped, calling it "standard practice." A drone hit central Kherson on Monday, damaging a medical facility. Separately, President Zelenskyy told Fox News that Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian refineries for a month if the U.S. supplied Patriot interceptors for that month.

Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile fired toward southern Saudi Arabia on Monday, the Saudi Defense Ministry said. Saudi Civil Defense issued warnings in Taif, Abha, Najran and Khamis Mushait as a precaution and lifted them after the threat passed. No casualties or target were reported. The Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked Saudi energy infrastructure in recent weeks.

Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat who lost Michigan's Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before the election. Stevens announced the endorsement after attending a service with Rogers at a Detroit church, the same day she was uninvited from a joint event with El-Sayed. "Abdul said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away, and he's right," she said in a video. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers." Stevens said she would vote for other Democrats and called her choice "more a statement about standing together against hate"; she has criticized El-Sayed for not doing enough to reassure Jewish and Black voters. El-Sayed told reporters, "I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," and said voters care about costs, schools and health care. Michigan Democrats condemned the move and President Trump praised it. The Trump-backed Rogers faces El-Sayed Tuesday in one of the races expected to decide Senate control.

The Justice Department's lawsuit to hold up certification of Alaska's Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses was dismissed Sunday by a federal judge; DOJ appealed. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage ruled the United States lacked standing and denied leave to amend, writing that the government offered "no workable plan" to set aside ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, a second candidate with a similar name, and investigate them while keeping votes secret. She added that ordering such a change on the eve of the election would likely confuse voters. The department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th Circuit the same day; a spokesperson said the court ruled on procedural grounds and "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election." A separate federal criminal probe into how Daniel J. Sullivan got on the ballot continues. Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola in Tuesday's ranked-choice election.

Binance reopened withdrawals in phases Sunday after its $6.3 billion hack, and customers pulled a net $3.6 billion in the first nine and a half hours. The exchange said it has covered 95% of the stolen assets and is still buying the less-liquid remainder, and that "Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds." Withdrawals restarted network by network, beginning with bitcoin, with some networks still partly suspended and delays expected. Between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC (1 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. ET) it processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1.0 billion in deposits, a net outflow equal to 2.1% of assets it holds, it said. The FBI said Saturday that the North Korean group TraderTraitor carried out the theft. Binance plans a proof-of-reserves report Monday and a fuller incident report later.

Zouhair Talbi was sixth in the fastest New York time by a U.S. man. Switzerland's Marcel Hug won the men's wheelchair race for an eighth time and Catherine Debrunner the women's. Bulgaria's acting president, Iliana Iotova, won Sunday's presidential runoff over former caretaker premier Andrey Gyurov, exit polls and early official results show. Five exit polls gave Iotova 50.7% to 52.5% against 43.4% to 44.7% for Gyurov, with pollsters calling a reversal highly unlikely; early Central Election Commission returns with about 17% of precincts counted had her near 58%. Turnout was under 30%. Iotova, 61, has served as acting head of state since Rumen Radev resigned in January; she favors dialogue with Moscow and opposes more military aid to Ukraine, while Gyurov backs Kyiv. She would be the first woman directly elected Bulgaria's president, a largely ceremonial post with a role in foreign policy and naming caretaker governments. Final results are due within three days.

Iran's talks with Qatari mediators ran a third straight day in Doha on Sunday with no deal, as Tehran's foreign minister urged U.S. "rationality." Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said talks on a "two-day proposal" were continuing but had reached no final conclusion; he said Saturday the plan would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of an agreement with Washington. An official briefed on the talks told Reuters they are coordinated with Washington. Trump said Sunday his Saturday call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "good"; Axios, citing a U.S. and an Israeli source, reported Netanyahu pressed for strikes right after Tuesday's midterms, which neither government confirmed. Trump has said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the vote.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, November 1, 2026
item.description:
The Golden State Valkyries won the WNBA championship in only their second season, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 Saturday in the first Game 7 in Finals history. Gabby Williams scored 30 points, 28 of them in the second half, and was named Finals MVP; she joined Penny Taylor (Phoenix, 2007) as the only players to score 30 or more in a winner-take-all Finals game. Golden State won the series 4-3 before 18,064 fans at Chase Center in San Francisco. Kiah Stokes had 13 rebounds and won her fourth title. For Atlanta, Jordin Canada scored 18, Allisha Gray 16, and Angel Reese had 8 points and 12 rebounds. It was Atlanta's fourth Finals loss.

Trump said Saturday that "one or two" Iranian nuclear sites remain and the U.S. could hit them "in ten minutes," while Rubio said no strike decision has been made. Speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago, Trump said the U.S. is "not in that much of a hurry" because it has "knocked down their Navy" and air force, mentioned the Pickaxe Mountain site, and said talks with Iran are "going fine" but Tehran is "not very reliable." Earlier Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, hosting G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, said Trump "hasn't made a decision" on resuming strikes and prefers a diplomatic solution. The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with it, reported that Trump spoke by phone with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday; neither government has described the call.

Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch was dismissed for good Saturday by a federal judge in Miami. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the amended suit with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled, ruling that Trump did not plausibly allege the Journal acted with actual malice, the standard set by the Supreme Court's 1964 New York Times v. Sullivan decision. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote, calling the paper's work a "thoughtful and detailed investigation." The suit was over a July 2025 story on a sexually suggestive letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album for Jeffrey Epstein's 50th birthday; Trump denies writing it. Gayles first dismissed the case in April and allowed an amended complaint, filed in May. The White House did not respond to AP's request for comment; CNBC reported Trump plans to appeal.

Iran designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force "terrorist" organizations and MI6 a "hostile group" on Sunday. The Iranian Foreign Ministry, in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA, said the step followed a Supreme National Security Council resolution and answered Britain's July 13 move to bring Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps under its State Threats Act 2026. Tehran also accused London of joining the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran by providing bases, and said the British government bears responsibility for the consequences. No British government response had been reported by early Sunday.

A "massive" Ukrainian drone attack overnight left an industrial plant in Russia's Kstovo district with "significant damage," the regional governor said; Ukrainian media said it was a major refinery. Nizhny Novgorod Gov. Gleb Nikitin said more than 100 drones were destroyed, there were no casualties according to preliminary information, and some homes could see temporary cuts to power, heat and hot water during repairs. He did not name the plant. Ukrainian media and war-monitoring channels identified it as Lukoil's Kstovo refinery (Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez). Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukraine had resumed refinery strikes after a pause, according to AFP.

Poland's court crisis deepened Saturday as President Karol Nawrocki pushed into the Constitutional Tribunal overnight, and crisis talks ended with no plan. Nawrocki, back from an aborted trip to Senegal, entered the tribunal around 1 a.m. Warsaw time and told judges backed by the current parliament, including Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, "You are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal"; Korwin-Piotrowska said he barged into them, and each side blames the other for the scuffle. In a statement read outside the court, he called it a "violation of the constitutional order," demanded police withdraw and called urgent talks citing "the threat to internal security." Those talks with several parties produced no joint plan; Prime Minister Donald Tusk's Civic Coalition and the Left stayed away. In an evening address, Tusk vowed "no compromise" on the rule of law and defended the newly elected judges. Police said three protesters were arrested Friday; the court's own X account called the moves a "coup," a word Law and Justice leaders also use.

Trump's planned 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" faces a new lawsuit from Virginia and the District of Columbia, filed days before construction is set to begin. Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued the National Park Service and the Interior Department in federal court in Washington on Saturday, asking for a temporary restraining order. They argue the arch at Memorial Circle, by Arlington Memorial Bridge and the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, lacks the approval from Congress that the Commemorative Works Act requires, would break D.C.'s 130-foot height limit, and skipped environmental and historic-preservation reviews. They say three years of construction would snarl traffic between the two jurisdictions and pollute the Potomac. The administration has said work could start as early as Nov. 5. It is the third suit against the arch; U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan heard arguments Friday in the first, brought by Vietnam veterans and a historian, and said she would rule quickly.

Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, ordered the armed forces to answer any threat immediately and "without geographic limits," with U.S. and Israeli assets added to target lists. Khamenei gave the order Saturday at a meeting with senior commanders, according to a statement on his website; he told them to update the military's target list to include U.S. and Israeli assets. Separately, Iranian state TV, citing a provincial official in Hormozgan, said U.S. forces attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, wounding one fisherman; two missing men were later found. The U.S. military has not confirmed the claim, and the White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Vice President JD Vance's letter a "positive step" but said Iran has no plans to meet U.S. officials, as an Iranian team holds talks with Qatari and Pakistani mediators in Doha.

Iranian strikes have damaged 274 structures at 24 bases used by U.S. forces, with repairs priced at $5 billion or more, a Wall Street Journal investigation found. The Journal's review of satellite imagery covered installations with a U.S. presence in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iraq. U.S. officials told the paper the Pentagon's internal estimate is at least $5 billion, and one assessment runs as high as $15 billion; those costs are not in the military's $47.1 billion war-cost estimate. After the July ceasefire collapsed, Iran increasingly targeted buildings housing troops, the Journal reported. The Pentagon has not publicly detailed the damage and declined to comment.

Early voting passed 52 million ballots heading into the final weekend before Tuesday's midterms, a record for a midterm election. The University of Florida Election Lab's tracker, last updated 4:31 p.m. Saturday, shows about 52.3 million early votes: about 28.9 million cast in person and 23.5 million mail ballots returned, with more than 60 million mail ballots requested. Reuters reported the total had already set a midterm record. Some states do not update daily, so the count will keep rising before Election Day, Nov. 3.

The G20 foreign ministers' meeting hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Atlanta ended without a joint statement, split over Russia's war in Ukraine. After two days of talks, Rubio released a chair's statement listing priorities, including energy security, supply chains and critical minerals, and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, but no agreements. "I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems," Rubio told reporters. The meeting opened Friday amid European objections to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov's presence; EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Lavrov of "a lot of lies." The U.S. holds the G20 presidency this year.

A shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store at a Fairfield, Calif., mall killed one person and wounded six, and the gunman was still being sought Saturday. Gunfire broke out about 8:30 p.m. Friday Pacific time at the Solano Town Center. Police said Saturday the shooting stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect and that detectives were reviewing video to identify the shooter; no one has been detained. One person died at the scene and three were critically injured. The FBI's Sacramento office sent an evidence team, and the mall canceled its Halloween trick-or-treat event.

Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reached Ukrainian-held territory Saturday under the local truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump. The convoy took a long route through Crimea and Russia into Belarus before crossing into Ukraine's Chernihiv region; it had room for about 750 people. Officials have not given a final count of how many chose Ukraine rather than Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the arrivals would get help and thanked the first lady. Fighting elsewhere went on: Zelensky said Russian strikes overnight left about 280,000 households without power.

item.description:

The Justice Department must stop threatening to prosecute election officials over alleged noncitizen voters, a federal judge ordered Friday, days before the midterms. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco issued a temporary restraining order barring the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding that election officials in any state segregate ballots, remove voters from the rolls or halt ballot processing based on the administration's lists of alleged noncitizen voters, and from threats of criminal prosecution. Officials who handle ballots in line with the law "do not violate federal criminal law" even if a voter is alleged to be ineligible, she wrote. The administration must also tell her about any search warrants or grand jury subpoenas seeking election materials tied to those lists. The order, in a suit by unions and civil rights groups including the NAACP and LULAC, expires Nov. 16. The Justice Department had no immediate comment.

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal plunged into crisis Friday as its president was suspended and police secured the court, and President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane back to Warsaw. A judge elected by the current parliament ordered the tribunal's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy to stop their duties; the tribunal's leadership called it illegal. Police were deployed after objects were thrown at officers during protests outside. Nawrocki, an ally of the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, cut short a flight to Senegal, saying the president "must be in Poland." Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek asked to lift the two judges' immunity, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said restoring the rule of law is the government's duty. PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski called it a coup; the U.S. ambassador urged restraint.

The State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine on Friday, paid for by allies, not U.S. funds. Canada, Germany and Norway are covering the cost through a U.S. program, along with Ukrainian funds financed by an EU loan, the department said; Lockheed Martin is the main contractor. The proposed sale goes to Congress for review, and no delivery schedule was announced. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is short of Patriot missiles to stop Russian ballistic missiles.

The Nasdaq fell 3.4% Friday, Wall Street's worst day since June, as Intel lost about 30% in its worst day since 1974. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,283.66, down 901.06 points, per Nasdaq, and is more than 8% below its Oct. 6 record close. The S&P 500 fell about 2% and the Dow about 1%, Reuters reported, and all three indexes posted a weekly loss. Intel fell after weaker-than-expected guidance that cited a plant shutdown in Israel and soft PC demand; AMD dropped about 12%, Nvidia about 5% and the chip index nearly 9%, while Amazon slipped about 2% after its earnings, on worries that AI spending is not yet paying off. The Nasdaq is headed for its worst month since early 2025.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia's best-known independent newspaper, said it will close on Nov. 9 after pressure from the authorities. In an editorial titled "They have killed us," the paper led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov blamed Russian authorities and security services, saying it received an eviction order and its reader-donation system was shut down. It plans one final issue. There was no immediate Kremlin comment, AP reported. The paper, founded in 1993, suspended print publication in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine; Novaya Gazeta Europe operates separately from abroad.

Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated in Brazil's runoff, reached Miami on Wednesday, Oct. 28, entering on one-year U.S. humanitarian parole after President Trump approved his entry. Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda and their two daughters crossed into Argentina at Puerto Iguazú at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday, Argentina's migration authority said, then took a private charter to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and flew on to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, landing about 9:30 a.m. ET, AP reported. A senior State Department official had said the U.S. would issue the family visas, and Trump said he approved, calling the election "really strange." U.S. Customs and Border Protection entry records reported by O Globo and CNN Brasil show the family was admitted under "DT" discretionary parole, a temporary humanitarian permission valid until Oct. 27, 2027 that is not a visa or asylum. Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to hand over his passports by noon Tuesday in corruption and money-laundering probes, and police canceled them when he did not. Bolsonaro, who denies wrongdoing, said: "I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil." President Lula called the departure "shameful."

College accreditors must focus on student outcomes and make viewpoint-neutral decisions under a final Education Department rule published Friday, effective July 1, 2027. Accreditors decide which colleges can take part in federal student aid, more than $100 billion a year in Pell Grants and loans, the department said. The rule, which carries out President Trump's executive order on accreditation, requires accreditor decisions to be neutral on viewpoint and ideology (except for agencies with a religious mission), says accreditors may not have standards that encourage race-based admissions targets, and adds reviews of student achievement, academic freedom and intellectual diversity. It makes it easier for colleges to switch accreditors or use more than one, drops geographic limits and the "two-year rule" for new accreditors, and adds a tougher review of the biggest institutional accreditors. Colleges must give students written reasons when they deny transfer credit, accept comparable credits and offer an appeal.

The Nasdaq fell 3.4% Friday, Wall Street's worst day since June, as Intel lost about 30% in its worst day since 1974. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,283.66, down 901.06 points, per Nasdaq, and is more than 8% below its Oct. 6 record close. The S&P 500 fell about 2% and the Dow about 1%, Reuters reported, and all three indexes posted a weekly loss. Intel fell after weaker-than-expected guidance that cited a plant shutdown in Israel and soft PC demand; AMD dropped about 12%, Nvidia about 5% and the chip index nearly 9%, while Amazon slipped about 2% after its earnings, on worries that AI spending is not yet paying off. The Nasdaq is headed for its worst month since early 2025.

Flu hospitalizations hit their highest rate for this point in the season since 2010-11, CDC's weekly report said Friday, with the first child death reported. In the week ending Oct. 24, the estimated hospitalization rate was 1.9 to 2.5 per 100,000 after accounting for reporting delays, CDC's FluView said; hospitals reported 6,100 flu admissions nationally. Nearly all cases are influenza A(H1N1). CDC estimates at least 1 million illnesses, 16,000 hospitalizations and 900 deaths so far this season. Flu activity is still low nationally but rising in many areas and higher than usual for October; CDC said an early start does not necessarily mean a worse peak. The first pediatric flu death of the 2026-27 season was reported this week.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia's best-known independent newspaper, said it will close on Nov. 9 after pressure from the authorities. In an editorial titled "They have killed us," the paper led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov blamed Russian authorities and security services, saying it received an eviction order and its reader-donation system was shut down. It plans one final issue. There was no immediate Kremlin comment, AP reported. The paper, founded in 1993, suspended print publication in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine; Novaya Gazeta Europe operates separately from abroad.

Treasury's new fraud measures, announced in Minnesota Friday, warn banks about $8 billion in suspicious overseas wire payments and charity scams. Speaking in St. Cloud alongside other senior officials, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Treasury has stopped nearly $190 million tied to overseas fraud and returned more than $100 million to U.S. victims. FinCEN issued an alert on more than $8 billion in potentially suspicious wire payments from 2021 to 2025 sent through U.S. money services businesses at the direction of foreign agents, and a notice on sham charities, fraud and embezzlement at nonprofits. Treasury also noted that Salim Said, a Feeding Our Future co-conspirator, was sentenced this week to 30 years in prison.

A former Fort Bragg security contractor is charged with posting classified military-operation images online and stealing Army night-vision goggles, the Justice Department said Friday. James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, N.C., was arrested Tuesday after an indictment was unsealed charging him with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and theft of government property. Prosecutors say he held a Top Secret/SCI clearance while working at the Army Special Operations Command facility, posted classified photos and videos to social media, and kept a classified award write-up and a missing unit night-vision system at home. An indictment is only an allegation.

Worker pay costs rose 0.8% in the third quarter, the Labor Department said Friday, but wages trailed inflation over the past year. Compensation costs for civilian workers rose 3.4% over the 12 months through September; wages and salaries rose 3.1% and benefits 3.9%. Adjusted for inflation, private-sector wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the year. Private health-benefit costs rose 6.4%. The Fed watches the Employment Cost Index as a gauge of wage-driven inflation.

ExxonMobil and Chevron beat profit forecasts Friday as high oil and diesel prices lifted third-quarter earnings. Exxon earned $15.4 billion, or $17.5 billion ($4.23 a share) excluding items, above the $4.12 analysts expected, on revenue of $113.16 billion; its Gulf Coast refineries ran at full capacity. Chevron earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, on $67.8 billion in revenue, with refineries at 98% utilization, the companies and AP reported.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 30, 2026
item.description:
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, lost about $6.3 billion to hackers in the largest crypto theft ever; blockchain firms blame North Korea. Most of the theft unfolded in about 20 minutes beginning late Thursday, Reuters reported. U.S. blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible; TRM tied it to TraderTraitor, the unit the FBI blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. There is no U.S. government attribution yet, and North Korea did not respond to Reuters. Binance halted withdrawals, said user funds are safe and that it will cover the losses, and expects withdrawals to resume within 48 hours; it said a hacked engineer's laptop may have been the entry point. About $3 billion has been located and frozen, including nearly $1.57 billion by Tether and more than $800 million by Circle. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 before steadying, and Coinbase shares fell 4.8%.

Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated in Brazil's runoff, reached Miami on Wednesday, Oct. 28, entering on one-year U.S. humanitarian parole after President Trump approved his entry. Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda and their two daughters crossed into Argentina at Puerto Iguazú at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday, Argentina's migration authority said, then took a private charter to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and flew on to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, landing about 9:30 a.m. ET, AP reported. A senior State Department official had said the U.S. would issue the family visas, and Trump said he approved, calling the election "really strange." U.S. Customs and Border Protection entry records reported by O Globo and CNN Brasil show the family was admitted under "DT" discretionary parole, a temporary humanitarian permission valid until Oct. 27, 2027 that is not a visa or asylum. Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to hand over his passports by noon Tuesday in corruption and money-laundering probes, and police canceled them when he did not. Bolsonaro, who denies wrongdoing, said: "I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil." President Lula called the departure "shameful."

College accreditors must focus on student outcomes and make viewpoint-neutral decisions under a final Education Department rule published Friday, effective July 1, 2027. Accreditors decide which colleges can take part in federal student aid, more than $100 billion a year in Pell Grants and loans, the department said. The rule, which carries out President Trump's executive order on accreditation, requires accreditor decisions to be neutral on viewpoint and ideology (except for agencies with a religious mission), says accreditors may not have standards that encourage race-based admissions targets, and adds reviews of student achievement, academic freedom and intellectual diversity. It makes it easier for colleges to switch accreditors or use more than one, drops geographic limits and the "two-year rule" for new accreditors, and adds a tougher review of the biggest institutional accreditors. Colleges must give students written reasons when they deny transfer credit, accept comparable credits and offer an appeal.

Israel's final election results show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority, winning 53 of 120 seats; no side has the 61 needed. The main opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48 seats and Arab-led parties a historic 19, after record Arab turnout. Netanyahu's Likud is the largest party with 27 seats, per the Central Elections Committee's final count reported by Ynet. Netanyahu stays in charge while parties negotiate; Israel's president will assign someone to try to form a government next week, and if no one can, a new election could be held early next year. Netanyahu's party has made unsubstantiated claims of election interference by Arab-led parties.

The Justice Department's probe of Alaska's second "Dan Sullivan" widened with grand jury subpoenas, including to Mary Peltola's campaign; Peltola denies knowing about the effort. A person familiar with the matter told AP that subpoenas for grand jury testimony or documents, plus records-preservation demands, went out after the New York Times reported Peltola's campaign appeared to help recruit Dan J. Sullivan Jr. onto the ballot; a source told Reuters there were more than 40, with more expected, including to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign. Separately on Thursday, the department amended its lawsuit in Anchorage federal court that seeks to block quick certification of a close Senate result, adding a constitutional claim and alleging Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee misled Judge Sharon Gleason. Alaska's elections division called that "gamesmanship," and the campaign and DSCC asked the judge to dismiss the case before Election Day. Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered state police to investigate. Peltola told voters in Juneau she "knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent," Sen. Dan Sullivan; her campaign says it has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.

Christine Lagarde will step down as European Central Bank president on Feb. 7, 2027, months before her term ends, the ECB announced Thursday. Lagarde, 70, told the ECB's Governing Council and European Council President António Costa, who said the process to pick her successor starts immediately; the European Council will appoint the next president under the EU treaty. She has led the ECB since November 2019, and her term was due to run until October 2027. She said she wants "the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters," Reuters reported. The same day, the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5%, pausing after a September hike even as energy costs push euro-zone inflation, now 3.8%, higher.

The 2027 diversity visa lottery can stay closed for now: a federal appeals court paused a judge's order forcing the State Department to open it. In a published order Thursday in Red Eagle Law v. Rubio, Ninth Circuit Judges M. Margaret McKeown, N. Randy Smith and Holly A. Thomas granted the government's emergency stay of the Oct. 14 injunction, which had required the department to announce registration by Oct. 29, open it by Nov. 1 and notify selectees by Dec. 3. The court said the government is likely to win because the immigration law firm that sued, the only plaintiff, is not within the program's zone of interests; Judge Smith, concurring, said the firm also had not shown standing. The stay lasts while the appeal continues. The program offers up to 55,000 green cards a year to people from countries with low immigration to the U.S.; the department had skipped the DV-2027 registration without explanation.

Amazon's cloud sales grew 39%, the fastest in nearly five years, but AI spending turned its free cash flow into a $42 billion yearly outflow. Third-quarter sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion and operating income reached $28.1 billion, a record 13.9% margin; Amazon Web Services revenue was $46.0 billion. Net income slipped to $20.7 billion ($1.89 a share) from $21.2 billion a year earlier, when it included gains on Amazon's Anthropic stake. Amazon still expects about $220 billion in capital spending this year and forecast fourth-quarter sales of $240 billion to $247 billion. Separately, Intel shares fell about 20% after hours when it forecast weaker fourth-quarter sales, citing a PC slowdown it expects to last at least through the first half of next year.

Patrick Stewart, the stage actor who played Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and Professor X in "X-Men," has died at 86. He died Wednesday at home in Los Angeles after "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said, with his wife, Sunny Ozell, at his side. A veteran of more than 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions, he won three Olivier Awards, was knighted in 2010 and reprised Professor X in "Avengers: Doomsday," due in December.

A Justice Department crackdown on "ghost student" fraud, which used stolen identities to collect federal student aid, has charged five people and seized $750,000 in crypto. Announced Thursday in Alexandria, Va., Operation Ghostbusters targets rings that filed fake FAFSA applications in the names of Americans whose identities were stolen, enrolled the "ghost students" and routed aid refunds through U.S. money mules to accounts tied to Kenyan nationals. Charges so far include three people arrested on a New Jersey complaint (about $1.5 million intended loss), a Kenyan national indicted Oct. 21 in Virginia (about $1.4 million) and a case in Nebraska. DOJ called the cryptocurrency seizure the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya. USA Today reported more than 40 open cases across 26 FBI field offices.

item.title: Evening Edition, Thursday, October 29, 2026
item.description:
A Trump administration rule narrowing who counts as "medically frail" under new Medicaid work requirements was struck down by a federal judge in Boston on Thursday. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns sided with 25 states and the District of Columbia, ruling that CMS unlawfully limited the exemption to people whose physical, mental or behavioral health condition "significantly impairs" their ability to meet the work requirement. He vacated that language and permanently barred its enforcement; California's attorney general said the order also gives the states a six-month stay of enforcement to absorb errors or delays from the changes. Stearns upheld other challenged parts of the rule, including a one-year look-back for diagnoses and one self-attestation per enrollment period. Under the 2025 law, most adults 19 to 64 must log 80 hours a month of work, community service or schooling to keep Medicaid starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the spring, while September inflation rose to 3.6%. The Bureau of Economic Analysis's advance estimate credited investment (led by business inventories and computer equipment), consumer spending and government spending, partly offset by lower exports. Sales to private domestic buyers rose at a 4.9% rate. In a separate report, the PCE price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year earlier; excluding food and energy, prices rose 0.3% on the month and 3.1% on the year. Personal income rose 0.2% and spending 0.5%, but inflation-adjusted spending was flat and the saving rate was 3.8%. The second GDP estimate is due Nov. 25.

Pharmacy benefit managers must disclose rebates, fees and spread-pricing profits to large employer health plans under a final Labor Department rule issued Thursday. The rule covers PBMs, and brokers and consultants affiliated with them, that serve self-insured plans generally with 100 or more participants or employees. They must disclose direct and indirect pay, including drugmaker rebates and fees, spread compensation, pharmacy clawbacks, price-protection payments and formulary-placement incentives, before a contract is signed or renewed and then every six months (quarterly on request). Plans may audit the disclosures at least once a year. It applies to plan years starting on or after July 1, 2027. The department projects about $22 billion in lower drug costs for employers and workers over 10 years, Healthcare Dive reported.

Immigration agents in Southern California may not stop people just for looking Latino or working-class, a federal judge ruled in an order made public Thursday. U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong's preliminary injunction, issued last week, requires individualized reasonable suspicion before an immigration stop. She cited "a mountain of evidence," including body-camera footage and agents' text messages using slurs for Latinos. The order covers Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties and exempts ports of entry and checkpoints. The Supreme Court stayed her earlier, broader order last year; she said the new request rests on different evidence and legal theories, and noted the ruling is not a final finding of an unlawful policy. The administration filed a notice of appeal to the 9th Circuit on Wednesday. DHS has denied racial profiling.

Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff's top planner fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, faces a Justice Department referral over alleged leaks, Pentagon officials say. Hegseth removed Sylvia this week as director for strategy, plans and policy (J5), the second general ousted from that post under Hegseth, as President Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Thursday that after "an extensive Air Force OSI investigation" the department took personnel action and referred the matter to the Justice Department for "potential further legal action," without naming Sylvia. A senior Pentagon official told ABC News and The Hill that Sylvia leaked classified information about the Iran and Ukraine wars to journalists and failed three polygraphs. The Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement thanking him for his service. Sylvia has not been charged, and no replacement has been named.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, October 29, 2026
item.description:
The Milwaukee Brewers won the first World Series title in franchise history, beating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 Wednesday night. Milwaukee took the Series four games to one at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla. Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings and rookie Cooper Pratt had two hits and two RBIs. Catcher William Contreras was named Series MVP after hitting .381 (8-for-21) with four RBIs; his sixth-inning RBI double scored Christian Yelich for a 3-0 lead. He threw out four would-be base stealers and won 10 of 13 challenges in the first World Series with automated ball-strike reviews. The Rays became the third team to lose their first three World Series.

The Trump administration's bid to make California set aside ballots from up to 20,000 suspected noncitizens was rejected by a federal judge Wednesday. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter wrote that holding the ballots "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway" and risk disenfranchising citizens, likening it to a voter purge barred within 90 days of an election. More than 3.7 million Californians have already voted. The Justice Department, which sued in mid-October saying counties missed a 48-hour deadline to review its list, appealed Wednesday evening. DOJ made a similar request in Washington state this week.

North Korea fired about a dozen short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast Thursday, South Korea's military said. The Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were launched from the Wonsan area around 12:30 p.m. local time and flew about 250 kilometers, with analysis under way with the United States. The launch came after Seoul offered talks to ease border tensions over a recent land mine blast. It follows another launch on Oct. 12.

The Federal Reserve held its key interest rate at 3.75% to 4% Wednesday, but two officials voted to raise it, saying inflation is still too high. The vote was 10-2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point increase. The statement says the economy is "expanding at a strong pace," job gains have kept pace with the workforce, inflation "remains elevated," and "the Committee will deliver price stability." At his news conference, Chair Kevin Warsh said energy prices have moved higher again and the Fed will fit its next move to incoming data. He also said the Fed will hold fewer rate-setting meetings: in 2027 one of its eight meetings will be devoted only to long-run strategy, and in 2028 two will be, leaving six for rate decisions. Separately, the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.50% Wednesday, its first increase since July 2023, citing higher, more persistent inflation and energy costs, and said more hikes may be needed.

Alphabet shares fell about 7% after hours as AI spending turned its free cash flow sharply negative, while Microsoft rose about 6% on faster cloud growth. Alphabet's third-quarter revenue rose 25% to $127.58 billion, its fastest growth since 2021, and Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion. But net income fell to $26.17 billion ($2.12 a share) from $34.98 billion, hurt by an $8.66 billion loss on equity holdings, and free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion; capital spending was $51.36 billion. Search revenue rose 12% to $63.35 billion, below estimates. Microsoft said revenue at its Azure cloud business grew 48% to $33.17 billion in the quarter ended September, above estimates. Reuters noted investor worry over Big Tech's debt-funded AI buildout, expected to top $700 billion this year.

Vice President JD Vance wrote to Iran's top security official seeking to restart talks, saying any negotiations "require discussions on the nuclear issue," a U.S. official said. The letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, was first reported by The Wall Street Journal; Axios, citing a U.S. official, called it the most senior U.S. outreach to Iran in several months. It comes as President Trump weighs resuming major combat operations after the midterms. Trump told reporters the letter was "basically" about getting medical supplies to people who are not well. Iran wants the U.S. naval blockade lifted and frozen funds released first; the U.S. wants nuclear talks before sanctions relief.

A high-speed train crash in central Spain killed at least 68 people Wednesday when one train slammed into another stopped on the Madrid-Seville line. A Renfe train hit the rear of an Iryo train halted at a red signal near Urda, in Toledo province, just before 9 a.m. local time; the two trains carried about 544 people. The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said 58 people were being treated in hospitals. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer communications failure had stopped traffic and that an "inexplicable" decision to let the Renfe train proceed caused the crash. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of mourning, and most parties paused campaigning for Spain's general election. It is Spain's deadliest rail crash since 2013 and the second high-speed collision on the line this year, after a January crash that killed 46. Toll as of Wednesday afternoon ET; it may rise.

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96. A family spokesperson told AP she died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, Calif., surrounded by family. Huerta co-founded the farmworkers' union with César Chávez in the 1960s, helped lead the national grape boycott and negotiated its first contracts, and spent decades organizing for labor, civil and women's rights. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. Earlier this year she said Chávez had sexually abused her in the 1960s. Gov. Gavin Newsom ordered flags at California's Capitol lowered in her honor.

Google's new top AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, is going first only to vetted cyber defenders because of its skill at finding and exploiting software flaws. Google says Carbon leads benchmarks for finding vulnerabilities, validating exploits and writing patches, and ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; those claims are Google's own. Access starts through Google's Fairwind program for security teams, and Google says it is taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release model testing. It will open to developers, businesses and consumers later, at introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. CEO Sundar Pichai said on Alphabet's earnings call Wednesday that Carbon outperforms its predecessor, Argon, "on almost every domain."

Mary Peltola's campaign aides and Senate Democrats' campaign arm helped recruit a second "Dan Sullivan" onto Alaska's ballot, the New York Times reported; both deny it. Citing interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a possible lawsuit, the Times reported that people working with Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee took part in a broader "ballot composition project" to recruit would-be spoilers, including Daniel J. Sullivan, to draw votes from Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved but was "definitely aware"; the Times said Rios later tried to retract her comments. Peltola's campaign said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," and the DSCC said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan." The Times noted ballot-stacking is common and generally legal. After the report, President Trump demanded that Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan be removed from the ballot. A Justice Department suit seeks to block certification of a close result; Judge Sharon Gleason has fast-tracked motions to dismiss it before the Nov. 3 election.

Congo's Ebola outbreak has passed 10,000 cases, with nearly 5,000 deaths, the World Health Organization said, making it the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Congo's Health Ministry counted 10,141 cases as of Monday. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, has spread to eight provinces; it is the largest of Congo's 17 Ebola outbreaks and second only to West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic. More than 2,600 people have recovered, and a ring-vaccination trial of the Ervebo vaccine has begun in Bunia. Kenya's count stays at nine cases and two deaths, all linked to its first imported case; 20 contacts have been released from quarantine. The U.N. allotted more than $2 million for Kenya's response. A CDC order announced Tuesday requires air travelers entering the U.S. to attest they have not been in Congo in the past 21 days.

The taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting President Trump were blocked again Wednesday, this time by a federal judge in Washington in the Democrats' lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan granted the Democratic National Committee a temporary restraining order barring the administration from developing, airing or distributing the ads, paused a $20 million Office of Management and Budget allocation for them, and ordered DHS and OMB to tell the contractor, LMD Agency, to stop. The order lasts 14 days. It has little practical effect before the Nov. 3 election because a federal judge in New York had already ordered the ads halted through Nov. 8 in a separate case.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, October 28, 2026
item.description:
The Biden-era methane rules for oil and gas wells would be loosened under an EPA proposal President Trump announced Tuesday at a Texas rally. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Trump unveiled the proposal in Lubbock. It would create separate, lighter standards for low-producing "marginal" wells (or, under a second option, for conventional wells), rescind the Super Emitter Program that let certified outside monitors flag large methane leaks, build a repair window into leak rules for covers and vent systems, and return to 95%-efficient flaring as the standard for gas from oil wells instead of requiring it to be piped to market. EPA says the changes would save $45 billion and add an estimated 210 million barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. It is a proposal: it takes effect only after a public comment period and a final rule. The 2024 rules, known as OOOOb/c, were estimated to cost $18 billion when finalized.

Israel's vote count puts Netanyahu's bloc ahead but short of a majority, with about three-quarters of ballot boxes counted and no clear winner. Partial Central Elections Committee results with 76.8% of ballot boxes counted (as of 10:58 a.m. Israel time) give Netanyahu's bloc 54 of the Knesset's 120 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 47 and the Arab-led Joint List and Ra'am 19; 61 are needed to govern. Likud is the largest party. Seat numbers are projections from vote shares and will shift: double-envelope ballots, including soldiers', are counted later. Netanyahu's bloc ran ahead of most exit polls, which had it near 50.

The Tampa Bay Rays avoided a World Series sweep, rallying for two runs in the 12th inning to beat the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 and force Game 5. Milwaukee led the series 3-0 and went ahead 3-2 on rookie Cooper Pratt's home run in the top of the 12th. In the bottom half, a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz put the leadoff man on, Jonny DeLuca's single tied it, and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson's bases-loaded chopper won it. The Rays are the fifth team down 3-0 in a World Series to win Game 4; the previous four lost Game 5. Game 5 is Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET at Tropicana Field.

Gulf Arab countries have been told by the U.S. to prepare for a possible "short, intense" military campaign against Iran after the midterms, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Journal, citing people briefed on the conversations, said the messages went through diplomatic and military channels; it reported that a Patriot missile-defense battery is moving from Texas to the region, troops have been moved from exposed bases, and another carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are expected next month. It said Trump has not made a final decision. The White House declined to comment on "sensitive military plans that may or may not exist" and said Trump "keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon." At his Lubbock, Texas, rally Tuesday, Trump said, "You'll see Iran in a couple of weeks." Separately, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the UN Security Council on Oct. 27 that his agency has seen no activity to repair Iran's nuclear sites damaged in the 2025 and 2026 strikes, but that Iran still has not given inspectors access to verify its roughly 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium.

Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide who testified against Trump about Jan. 6, will not be indicted after a grand jury refused, people familiar with the case say. A federal grand jury in Washington rejected the Justice Department's request Tuesday, two people familiar with the matter told the AP. The case, handled by DOJ's Civil Rights Division, centered on her 2022 testimony to the House Jan. 6 committee, including her account that Trump lunged for the steering wheel of his vehicle, which Secret Service officials disputed. In a hearing on another matter, a division lawyer told a magistrate judge the grand jury had not agreed to a proposed indictment without naming the defendant. The refusal does not bar prosecutors from trying again. It is the latest grand jury rebuff in cases against people Trump has called political enemies.

Israel's election produced no clear winner, exit polls show, with neither Netanyahu's bloc nor his opponents near the 61 seats needed to govern. Polls closed at 10 p.m. Israel time (4 p.m. ET). Exit polls from Channels 11, 12 and 13 gave Netanyahu's bloc 50 of the Knesset's 120 seats and the Jewish-led opposition bloc 52 or 53. Netanyahu's Likud was projected as the largest party with 24 to 25 seats, ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! at 21 to 23. Arab-led parties were projected to win a record 17 or 18 seats, up from 10. Pro-government Channel 14 and i24 News showed better numbers for Netanyahu's bloc (60 and 55). Turnout was unusually high. The Central Elections Committee is counting votes, and official results can differ from exit polls; President Isaac Herzog will decide who gets the first chance to form a government, a process that could take weeks.

A CDC order will require every air passenger flying into the U.S. to sign a statement that they have not been in Congo in the past 21 days. The order, signed Oct. 22 and published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, applies to flights departing at or after 11:59 p.m. EST on Nov. 3 and runs through Dec. 18 unless changed. It covers every flight landing in the U.S., including connections; airlines must keep each signed statement for 42 days, and knowingly false statements can be prosecuted. Medical-evacuation flights and people CDC exempts on humanitarian grounds are excluded. CDC says Congo's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak had reached 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths as of Oct. 18; the order adds to the entry suspension already in place. Separately, a Swiss woman with Ebola diagnosed in Nigeria was flown to Geneva University Hospitals on Monday and is stable, Geneva health officials said.

The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system has been offline since Monday night after hacking attempts, a week before the midterms, Reuters reported. An FEC electronic filings officer wrote in an email seen by Reuters: "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web facing services." The FEC's status page says filing has been down since about 10 p.m. ET Monday; in a statement the agency said only that the system is offline and its IT staff are working to restore it, and declined to say what caused it. Past reports can still be searched. The outage blocks the 24- and 48-hour reports that show late spending by super PACs and other groups. The FEC does not run elections, and voting is not affected. CISA referred questions to the FEC; the FBI did not immediately comment.

A Biden-era rule letting immigration judges pause some deportation cases stays thrown out after the Supreme Court declined to restore it Tuesday. In a brief unsigned order in City of Baltimore v. Texas (No. 26A500), with no noted dissents, the court refused to pause a June consent judgment between Texas and the Justice Department that vacated the 2024 "administrative closure" rule. Chief Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls entered that judgment the same day Texas sued, at both parties' request. Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and Centro Legal de la Raza, which called the deal collusive, were denied permission to join the case; their appeal continues at the 5th Circuit.

U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuba's foreign minister got into a shouting match at the UN General Assembly during debate on the U.S. embargo. As Waltz accused Havana's leaders of corruption, the Cuban delegation interrupted, and Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez accused him of lying and demanded a point of order; the session was briefly suspended. The assembly votes Wednesday on its annual nonbinding resolution condemning the embargo, which passed 165-7 with 12 abstentions last year. The clash follows Secretary of State Marco Rubio's Oct. 23 public call for Cubans to work with the CIA.
